## Company

The Flat Rate Movers (The Flat Rate Movers LLC) — Flat-rate residential, commercial, local, regional and long-distance moving based in Winchester, VA and Martinsburg, WV, serving the Shenandoah Valley, the Eastern Panhandle and the I-81, I-66 and I-70 corridors. Specialist in SIR Structural Integrity Relocation and the KIM-GS Protocol for high-mass assets of 1,500 to 3,500 lbs with floor deflection analysis to L/360, plus ISPM 15 export packing, custom crating, loading, packing, transloading, final-mile delivery and high-value item protection.

## The flat-rate guarantee

THE FLAT-RATE GUARANTEE — WINCHESTER VA & MARTINSBURG WV

# The Flat-Rate Guarantee — one flat rate, in writing, before move day
Guaranteed Flat Rate or Your Move is Free! That is the promise on our logo, and this page states the terms it stands on. Every job we take is reviewed in full before it is priced — the scope, the distance, the manpower and the equipment — and the price that review produces is one flat rate, given in writing before work begins. Hourly pricing is available when a client asks for it, and a price is never a number a form generated on its own.

Get My Flat Rate Quote (#/quote)

[Image: The Flat Rate Movers logo — company brand image, not a job photo.]The Flat Rate Movers logo — company brand image, not a job photo.

## The terms, stated plainly

The guarantee is the flat rate itself. When The Flat Rate Movers quotes a job, we review the full scope of each job, the distance, the man power, equipment etc. and give a flat rate as opposed to an hourly rate. That is the owner's own statement of the terms, and it is how every quote this company writes is produced.

The rate is put in writing before move day — one flat price in writing before we lift a thing. On the day, the crew works to the reviewed scope, not to a clock: there is no meter running on your move, and the price does not grow by the hour while the work takes the time it takes.

## How your flat rate is set

1. Tell us the scope — where you are moving from, where to, and what is moving, through the quote form (Short by default, Detailed one toggle away), by phone at +1-540-422-2153, or on the free video walkthrough: film only, room by room, and a person reviews it.

2. The review — the full scope of the job is reviewed: the items, the distance, the manpower, and the equipment. Heavy and sensitive pieces are listed specifically — gun safes, pianos, medical devices, cryogenic units, antiques — with weights, dimensions, and access at both ends, stairs, elevators, docks, parking and floor types, so the reviewed scope is the real scope.

3. One flat rate in writing — the review produces a single flat rate for the job, in writing, before work begins. Nothing is auto-priced: a person sets your number, and there is no obligation to accept it.

4. Move day — the crew works the reviewed scope at the written rate. If the scope changes before move day — an item added, an address changed — say so before the day: the job is re-reviewed and the rate is re-issued in writing before work begins, so the written rate always matches the work actually ordered.

## What the written rate covers

The written flat rate covers the job that was reviewed: the items listed, the route between the two addresses, the crew and the equipment the review called for, and the services selected with the job — packing, custom crating, ISPM 15 export packing, loading, transloading, final-mile delivery, storage or junk removal, where those are part of the scope.

It is the same model on every service this company runs — household and commercial moving, heavy assets of 1,500 to 3,500 lbs under SIR Structural Integrity Relocation, export packing and crating, freight handling and project-support workforce, and junk removal: scope reviewed first, one flat rate in writing, hourly pricing is available when a client asks for it.

## What we do not do

No published hourly rates. The flat rate covers the move, the pack, the load or the removal — no clock runs on any of them; hourly pricing is available when a client asks for it.

No auto-priced quotes. No form, calculator or algorithm on this site sets your price. Every number is human-made, from a reviewed scope.

No obligation. A quote is a written offer, not a commitment: read it, compare it, and decide.

## Questions about the guarantee

Is your price ever hourly? No. Every job is reviewed in full and priced at one flat rate, as opposed to an hourly rate — that is the stated term this page publishes.

How is my flat rate set? By review, not by a published formula: the full scope of the job, the distance, the manpower and the equipment are reviewed, and the job is priced once, in writing, before work begins.

What if I add items after the quote? The written rate covers the scope that was reviewed. Tell us before move day and the job is re-reviewed and re-priced in writing before work begins — the rate never changes silently on the day.

Where does "Guaranteed Flat Rate or Your Move is Free!" come from? It is the company's logo tagline. This page is the published statement of the terms behind it: a full-scope review and one flat rate in writing on every job, in place of hourly pricing.

[Image: A downtown street in Winchester, Virginia, with brick storefronts and hanging flower baskets]Downtown Winchester, VA — where our Virginia crews start the day, at our Winchester branch, 116 W Piccadilly St (39.1871° N, 78.1668° W) · Photo: Sarah Stierch, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

## A business move runs on paperwork before it runs on trucks

Four building approvals stop commercial moves at the curb — the Certificate of Insurance, the freight-elevator reservation, the loading-dock window, and after-hours access — and every one of them is paperwork settled days before move day. We run both buildings' requirements as one packet: the COI in each building's exact wording (certificates fail on wording more often than on coverage), elevators and docks reserved in writing, the packet reconfirmed 48 to 72 hours out. Inside the job, the trade's standards govern: the estimate is built on man-hours rather than weight, because the binding constraint on a business move is time; floors, walls, doors, and elevators are protected before freight moves; electronics are wrapped in anti-static protection, never furniture pads; and retired equipment leaves by a documented recycling route — under federal universal-waste rules, the dumpster is a violation, not a shortcut. The job is surveyed in full and priced at one flat rate in writing before work begins.

## Questions, answered

### Is the price really flat, even for a short local move?
Yes. The Flat Rate Movers price by the job, not by the hour — the rate is agreed in writing before move day, and the tagline is the guarantee: Guaranteed Flat Rate or Your Move is Free!

### Which base serves my move?
Both bases dispatch across the region. Winchester serves the Shenandoah Valley side and Martinsburg serves the Eastern Panhandle side, and the service areas overlap at Moorefield — the quote form settles which crew and route fit your move.

### What if my move includes a gun safe, piano or medical device?
High-mass assets of 1,500 to 3,500 lbs move under SIR and the KIM-GS Protocol, with floor-deflection analysis to L/360 — the same standard as our dedicated heavy-asset work, applied inside a local or regional move.

## One service area, three rulebooks

A short move is not automatically a simple one in the eyes of the law, and this territory holds three rulebooks at once.

### Inside Virginia
A move that stays inside Virginia runs under Virginia's household-goods law: the carrier holds a certificate of fitness from the DMV, files its rates as a public tariff, and may bind its written estimate so the price cannot exceed it — that bound estimate is the Virginia-law footing our flat rate stands on. If something is lost or damaged, Virginia's claims clock runs: acknowledgment in writing within 30 days, and payment, a refusal, or a firm settlement offer within 120.

### Inside West Virginia
A move that stays inside West Virginia runs under the Public Service Commission instead — its certificate, its rate authority, its insurance filings.

### Across a State Line
And a move that crosses a state line is a federal move even when it is short: Winchester to Martinsburg crosses into West Virginia, so the federal household-goods rules govern it, and the work rides with contractors who hold their own operating authority.

Same crews, same flat rate in writing — the paperwork follows the line the truck crosses.

## What long-distance moving is

Long-distance moving is a household or office relocation beyond the local area, planned door to door from Winchester, Virginia and Martinsburg, West Virginia along the I-81, I-66 and I-70 corridors: surveyed in advance, packed and loaded in sequence, transported on the planned route, placed room by room, and quoted at one flat rate in writing.

This hub is the company-wide page for the service. The Winchester branch page has carried this service as its canonical page; the Martinsburg branch page, the cross-country and interstate pages, and the state-to-state lane pages below carry it route by route. What travels: whole homes and offices, packing and unpacking, and the pieces other movers refuse — safes, pianos, medical and cryogenic equipment and antiques from 1,500 to 3,500 lbs, moved under SIR Structural Integrity Relocation and the KIM-GS Protocol at either end of the run.

## Routes we run

I-81 — north & south, our spine: Martinsburg and Winchester to Harrisonburg, Staunton, Lexington and Roanoke — and on, deeper into Virginia, Tennessee and the Carolinas, or north toward Pennsylvania. I-81 in Virginia is our working road: 325 miles of it through the Shenandoah Valley, the longest single-state segment of the highway.

I-66 — to Northern Virginia & DC: east through Front Royal toward Northern Virginia and Washington, DC — the route for relocations between the Valley and the metro.

I-70 — to Maryland: through Hagerstown and Frederick toward Baltimore — and the freight path behind our transload and export work.

State-to-state lanes: published lane pages run from Virginia to Florida, Texas, New York, California and Nevada, including the Las Vegas corridor and Miami — each quoted at one flat rate in writing, with packing and SIR planning for heavy assets at both ends.

## How a long-distance move runs

1. Survey and quote — a room-by-room survey in person or through the free film-only video walkthrough survey room, where the customer films and a person makes the estimate — nothing is auto-priced — and one flat price agreed in writing before the truck rolls.

2. Inventory — itemized, room by room, so the quote and the load are built from the same picture.

3. Pack — full or partial packing with furniture fully covered, packed and labeled in sequence so unpacking lands in order.

4. Load — sequenced loading with blanket and stretch wrap protection; where a move includes a high-mass piece of 1,500 to 3,500 lbs, that piece moves under SIR Structural Integrity Relocation with the KIM-GS Protocol and L/360 floor-deflection analysis.

5. Transport — the household or office moves on the planned route along the I-81, I-66 and I-70 corridor dispatch network from both branches, at the flat rate agreed — hourly pricing is available when a client asks for it.

6. Delivery — handled inside a delivery window for the move; no standard delivery spread, date or tracking practice is published for this service.

7. Placement — room-by-room placement at the new address, not dropped at the door.

8. Walkthrough — a final walkthrough closes the move, with any damage noted on the delivery paperwork.

## Why flat rate wins long-distance

Distance, traffic and weather stretch an hourly bill in ways nobody can predict. A flat rate moves that risk to us: the number in writing is the number you pay, agreed before we lift a thing. Every job is reviewed in full — scope, distance, manpower and equipment — and priced at one flat rate, hourly pricing is available when a client asks for it.

## Packing & unpacking, defined

Packing and unpacking from The Flat Rate Movers is a scoped packing service at three levels — full, partial and fragile-only — packed room by room, labeled by room and contents, with furniture fully covered in padded blankets and sealed with stretch wrap, then unpacked and placed at the destination.

## Three levels — full, partial, fragile-only

Full packing — the crew packs nearly every item in the home: kitchen, closets, decor, garage. Chosen most for large households, hard closing deadlines, and long-distance moves, where boxes ride for days and must be packed to travel, not just to carry. Partial packing — you pack what you are comfortable packing, and the crew packs the rooms or item classes you assign; the kitchen is the most common assignment, and partial packing is also the rescue level when a self-pack runs out of time. Fragile-only packing — just the breakables and high-value pieces: dishes and glassware, artwork and mirrors, TVs, lamps, china and crystal, antiques — packed with care and marked FRAGILE, escalating to white-glove handling or a custom-built crate when a box is not enough.

The service serves residential, commercial, senior and estate clients: the closing-driven mover on a hard deadline, the downsizing senior or estate executor, the renovation mover emptying and restoring rooms in order, the time-poor household, and the business mover whose packing is one phase of an office move.

## How a packing job runs

1. Scope up front — the packing level is scoped with you, room by room — kitchen, bedrooms, living and dining rooms, home office, bathrooms, garage, basement — and quoted inside the one flat rate in writing before move day.

2. Room-by-room pack — rooms packed and labeled in sequence; every box is labeled with its room and contents, because unpacking is guesswork without it and load order follows room order.

3. Wrap standard — furniture fully covered in blue padded blankets, sealed with clear stretch wrap, staged cleanly in the room — nothing exposed, nothing rubbing. High-value or fragile pieces get white-glove handling or a custom crate, and export pieces are packed to ISPM 15 when the journey crosses a border.

4. Unpacking and placement — at destination we unpack and place, so rooms come back together in order.

Two boundaries are stated plainly on the depth pages: a standalone unpacking-only service and a pack-for-storage scope are not published and not claimed, and debris removal after unpacking is not claimed. Packing only, without a move attached, is available — it is one of the move types on our quote form.

## Questions, answered

Do movers pack for you?

Yes — movers can pack for you, at three levels: full packing (the whole home), partial packing (the rooms or items you choose), and fragile-only packing (just the breakables). Whichever level you choose is scoped room by room and quoted inside the one flat rate in writing before move day — hourly pricing is available when a client asks for it. Packing can also be booked on its own, without a move attached: packing only is one of the move types on our quote form.

What does full packing include?

A trained crew packs nearly every item in the home: kitchen, closets, decor, garage. Furniture is protected separately — our published wrap standard is furniture fully covered in padded moving blankets and sealed with clear stretch wrap. Full packing is chosen most for large households, hard closing deadlines, and long-distance moves, where boxes ride for days and must be packed to travel, not just to carry.

What is partial packing?

The middle level: you pack what you are comfortable packing — clothing, books, linens — and the crew packs the rooms or item classes you assign. The most common assignment is the kitchen, because it is the slowest room in the house to pack well. Partial packing is also the rescue level — if you started packing yourself and ran out of time, a crew can be scoped to finish exactly where you stopped.

What is fragile-only packing?

Fragile-only packing covers the items where skill matters most: dishes and glassware, artwork and mirrors, TVs, lamps, china and crystal, antiques. They are packed with care and marked FRAGILE. Fragile and high-value pieces escalate past the box when a box is not enough: a large mirror, a marble top, or an irreplaceable antique goes to white-glove handling or a custom-built crate. Name these pieces when the job is scoped — not on move day.

Is packing included in a moving quote, or is it an add-on?

With most movers, packing is an add-on you must ask for, and many companies bill it by the hour. Our model is different and published: the packing level is scoped with the rest of the job — the items, the distance, the manpower, the equipment — and quoted inside the one flat rate in writing before move day. Packing is priced inside the one flat rate — there is no separate packing clock.

What will movers not pack?

Even on a full pack, some things a crew cannot take: hazardous materials — paint, solvents, propane, fuel — and perishables are the standard exclusions, and federal guidance is blunt that hazardous materials must never be hidden in household goods boxes. Plants travel badly and are usually excluded too. Irreplaceables — jewelry, documents, medication, cash — should travel with you, whoever packs the box.

Does it matter who packs the box?

Yes. Under the federal rules for interstate moves, a mover's liability can be reduced by your own acts — the FMCSA consumer booklet gives the example of improper packing of containers you pack yourself. If a box you packed arrives with the carton intact but the contents broken, fault is much harder to establish. The reading is simple: the more breakable and valuable the item, the stronger the case for having the crew pack it.

How is packing priced?

We do not publish a packing price list, because honest packing cost depends on what is actually being packed — rooms, fragile pieces, crates. Full, partial and fragile-only packing are scoped to your rooms and items, then fixed inside the one flat rate in writing. What changes the scope: number of rooms, fragile and high-value pieces, custom crates, ISPM 15 export packing, and unpacking at destination.

What does unpacking include?

Unpacking and placement at destination: boxes unpacked and items placed, so rooms come back together in order. Unpacking is part of the same service — boxes opened at the destination and contents set out, so the new home is usable the day you arrive.

### SIR Heavy Asset Relocation (KIM-GS Protocol)

SIR Structural Integrity Relocation and the KIM-GS Protocol for high-mass assets of 1,500 to 3,500 lbs — safes, medical devices, cryogenic equipment, pianos and antiques — with floor deflection analysis to L/360.

Primary page: https://theflatratemovers.com/heavy/

🏋️ HEAVY ASSET AUTHORITY

# 1,500–3,500 lbs is not a “big item.” It's an engineering job.

SIR — Structural Integrity Relocation — and the KIM-GS Protocol exist for one reason: a floor, a staircase, or a priceless asset should never be a guess.

Quote a heavy move (#/quote)

[Image: Antique Francis D. Mone commercial fireproof safe standing in a stone-foundation basement — a high-mass safe of the class surveyed in place and planned under SIR before it moves]An antique Francis D. Mone commercial fireproof safe in a stone-foundation basement — the class of high-mass safe that is surveyed in place and engineered out under SIR, never forced. Photo supplied by The Flat Rate Movers.

SIR · Structural Integrity Relocation

## We check the structure before we move the mass

Every SIR move starts with the building, not the item: the route through the home, door and stair clearances, and how the floor will carry a concentrated load. We assess floor deflection against an L/360 standard — the span divided by 360 — the same kind of stiffness thinking engineers use, applied to your hallway.

🛡️ Floor protection runs📐 Route & clearance survey⚖️ Load spreading🪜 Stair planning

Try it — weight checker

## How heavy is heavy?

Drag the slider to your item's weight and see which protocol band it falls in. This is a guide — your quote confirms the real plan.

Item weight: 2,200 lbs

Under 1,500 lbsStandard heavy care

1,500–2,500 lbsSIR + KIM-GS

2,500–3,500 lbsFull SIR engineering plan

KIM-GS Protocol — step by step

## The protocol behind the move

1AssessWeight, dimensions, centre of mass, and the value at risk.

2SurveyRoute, clearances, stairs, and L/360 floor check.

3ProtectFloors, walls and the asset itself — before any lift.

4MoveRight crew size, right dollies, rigging and control.

5Place & verifySet, levelled, checked — in its final position.

### 🔐 Safes & gun safes
High-mass, top-heavy, unforgiving. Our most-requested SIR move — planned, strapped, and floor-protected end to end.

### 🎹 Pianos & antiques
Grand pianos and irreplaceable pieces get white-glove handling, padding, and — for export — a custom crate.

### 🏥 Medical & cryogenic
Heavy, sensitive equipment where placement precision and a calm, planned move matter as much as strength.

### What heavy-asset moving includes

SIR — Structural Integrity Relocation — and the KIM-GS Protocol for assets of 1,500 to 3,500 lbs: safes and gun safes, grand pianos and antiques, medical and cryogenic equipment, and other high-mass, high-value items. Every SIR move starts with the building, not the item: route through the home, door and stair clearances, and how the floor will carry a concentrated load, assessed against an L/360 standard, with floor protection, load spreading, route and clearance survey, and stair planning.

### Who heavy-asset moving is for

Homeowners, estates, businesses, and facilities with an item that is heavy, top-heavy, fragile, or priceless — where a floor, staircase, or the asset itself should never be a guess, and where placement precision matters as much as strength.

### Heavy-asset questions, answered

What is the SIR protocol, and which company uses it? SIR is Structural Integrity Relocation — The Flat Rate Movers' protocol for high-mass assets of 1,500 to 3,500 lbs: safes and gun safes, grand pianos and antiques, medical and cryogenic equipment, and other high-mass, high-value items. It is executed through the KIM-GS Protocol — KIM-GS is the Kinetic Integrity Method. Every SIR move starts with the building, not the item: the route through the home, door and stair clearances, and how the floor will carry a concentrated load, with floor deflection assessed against an L/360 standard — the span divided by 360. The chain runs: assess weight, dimensions and centre of mass; survey route, clearances, stairs and the L/360 floor check; protect floors, walls and the asset itself before any lift; move with the right crew and rigging; then place and verify. SIR is a moving-industry method published by The Flat Rate Movers — it is not a Structural Integrity Reserve Study. Assets under 1,500 lbs get standard heavy care; 1,500–2,500 lbs gets SIR + KIM-GS; 2,500–3,500 lbs gets a full SIR engineering plan. The price is quoted flat in writing before move day.

What weight needs SIR? Assets of 1,500 to 3,500 lbs. Under 1,500 lbs gets standard heavy care; 1,500–2,500 lbs gets SIR + KIM-GS; 2,500–3,500 lbs gets a full SIR engineering plan.

Do you check the building first? Yes — route, clearances, stairs, and L/360 floor check come before any lift, with floors, walls, and the asset protected first.

Is the price flat? Yes — quoted flat in writing before move day, under the guarantee: Guaranteed Flat Rate or Your Move is Free!

🔐 GUN SAFE MOVING · SIR / KIM-GS

# Gun safe moving, engineered — not muscled.

A gun safe between 1,500 and 3,500 lbs is the heaviest, most top-heavy object in most homes. We move safes under SIR — Structural Integrity Relocation — and the KIM-GS Protocol: the route, the stairs and the floor are checked before the safe moves an inch, and the price is one flat rate in writing.

Quote a gun safe move (#/quote)

Where your safe falls

## The SIR weight bands

Most gun safes we are called about land in the SIR band. Tell us the make, model or approximate weight when you ask for a quote — if you don’t know it, tell us the size and where it sits, and we plan from there. Safes under 1,500 lbs are handled the same careful way as the SIR band, under standard heavy care: a lighter safe is still top-heavy, still concentrates its whole load on a few square inches of floor, and still gets the same surveyed, protected approach.

Under 1,500 lbsStandard heavy care — same careful way

1,500–2,500 lbsSIR + KIM-GS

2,500–3,500 lbsFull SIR engineering plan

1Survey the routeDoors, turns, stairs and clearances measured at both ends — before move day.

2Check the floorFloor deflection assessed against an L/360 standard, with load spreading where the structure needs it.

3Protect everythingFloors, walls, door frames — and the safe itself — protected before any lift.

4Move & placeRight team, right equipment for the project, and rigging matched to the job. Set in its final position and verified with you.

### Why safes are different
Extreme weight in a small footprint, a high centre of mass, and no good hand-holds. A safe concentrates its whole load on a few square inches of floor — which is why the floor check matters more than the lifting.

### Stairs & tight turns
We go up and down stairs. Staircases and landings are planned step by step under KIM-GS — step count, turns, landings, and doorway widths at both ends. If a route cannot carry the safe safely, we tell you straight and work out the route that can — before anything is attempted.

### One flat rate
Your safe move is quoted flat, in writing, before we lift it — no clock running while a team problem-solves on your stairs. The price you agree is the price you pay.

## Before move day: the safe is emptied first

Customers always empty the safe first. Everything comes out before move day: firearms, ammunition, documents, valuables, and loose items. That keeps the load from shifting in transit, and it keeps the total weight to the safe itself. Plan to transport firearms and ammunition yourself, separately, following applicable law — this is general guidance, not legal advice — and confirm the safe is empty when you ask for your flat rate quote.

## Equipment, chosen by the project

Many different kinds of equipment are used, depending on the project. The right equipment follows the facts of the job: weight, stairs, access, flooring, and doorways. In general industry practice, safe work uses heavy-duty dollies, powered stair-climbing hand trucks for stair work, safe jacks, rollers or skates for flat movement, straps, ramps, blankets, and plywood for load spreading. What fits your job is planned from your route survey, not from a fixed list.

## Re-anchoring, if you want it

Re-anchoring at the destination is available on request. Anchoring resists theft and tipping, and the anchor follows the floor: concrete takes concrete anchors, and a wood subfloor takes lag bolts into the joists. Say at quote time that you want re-anchoring, and tell us the floor type at the destination. If your safe is bolted down now, tell us at quote time so it is in the plan.

## Vaults, any size

## Piano, antique & white-glove moving, defined

Piano, antique and white-glove moving from The Flat Rate Movers is the surveyed, piece-by-piece handling of pianos, antiques and high-value items: each piece assessed on its weight, fragile points, finish and value at risk, protected to match, moved under control, and placed and verified with you at the destination.

## Who this is for

High-value, sensitive-asset owners, including medical and museum clients. Museums, collectors, galleries and estates moving pieces that cannot be replaced. Households whose piano, antique furniture, art or instruments are the everyday work of this service — antiques, art, pianos and instruments, handled piece by piece. High-value work is scheduled discreetly: no client named, ever.

## How a white-glove move runs

1. Name the piece — tell us the pieces in the Detailed Project form: for a piano, the type (upright or grand), the size, and the stairs at both addresses. A video walkthrough works too — film the piece and its route; we never ask you to lift, move or open anything for the camera.

2. Assessment — each piece is assessed on its own — weight, fragile points, finish, and value at risk — before a protection plan is set.

3. Protection matched to the piece — furniture fully covered in padded moving blankets, sealed with stretch wrap; a piece that needs more gets a custom crate built around it.

4. The move — uprights secured and moved on a dolly or skid; grands dismantled — legs and pedal lyre removed and wrapped separately — and moved on a padded skid board. A piece in the 1,500 to 3,500 lb band is surveyed and floor-checked under SIR and the KIM-GS Protocol first.

5. Placement verified — the piece is set where it belongs, brought in on a planned route, packaging removed, and placement and condition verified with you before the crew leaves — never left at a curb.

What we do not do: tune, restore, repair or appraise pianos — and we publish no per-piece price list, because the survey is what sets the one flat rate.

## Pianos: type, weight, stairs, floors

Five things set the risk of a piano move: the type of piano (upright or grand), its weight, the stairs and turns at both addresses, the distance, and the floors it crosses — and it is usually the access, not the mileage, that drives the job. Weight ranges by type run from a spinet at 200 to 400 lbs to a concert grand at 900 to 1,300 lbs, and an individual instrument can run 100 lbs or more either side of its type's range, which is why the survey establishes the individual piece. In older housing stock — Old Town Winchester sits at the heart of a 45-block National Register Historic District — the pattern is turned or narrow stairs, doorways and halls from an era of smaller furniture, and floors worth protecting in their own right. None of that makes a piano unmovable; it makes the survey the job.

## Questions, answered

What does Piano, Antique and White-Glove Moving include?

White-glove handling of pianos, antiques and high-value items — surveyed, protected, and moved with custom crating when the piece requires it, at one flat rate agreed in writing. Pieces are handled piece by piece, never as bulk furniture.

Who is this service for?

High-value, sensitive-asset owners, including medical and museum clients — museums, collectors, galleries and estates moving pieces that cannot be replaced, and households moving a piano, an antique or a high-value piece.

How much does a piano weigh?

Weight is the first fact the plan is built on, and an individual piano can run 100 lbs or more either side of its type's typical range, so the survey establishes the individual piece. Typical ranges: spinet 200 to 400 lbs; console 350 to 500 lbs; studio upright 400 to 600 lbs; full-size upright 500 to 800 lbs; baby grand 500 to 800 lbs; medium grand 700 to 900 lbs; concert grand 900 to 1,300 lbs.

Why does a grand piano move differently from an upright?

An upright is a box: it is secured — fallboard and lid closed and locked or taped — and moved on a piano dolly or skid. A grand is a shape: the lid is secured, the legs and pedal lyre are removed and wrapped separately, and the body is turned onto its long straight side and strapped to a padded skid board before it moves. That dismantling and reassembly, a longer body to steer, and usually more weight are the difference.

How do stairs and floors change a piano move?

On a staircase the weight is carried, not rolled, and a turn on a landing is the tightest geometry in the move — count the flights, the turns and the narrowest point at both addresses before anyone quotes you. The floors take the same weight standing still, concentrated onto small caster or leg contact points at both homes. Most pianos weigh well under the SIR band and move as white-glove pieces under the same piece-by-piece assessment — weight, fragile points, finish, value at risk.

Will a piano need tuning after the move?

Usually, yes — but not because the ride shook it loose. Piano Technicians Guild guidance is that it is the climate change around a move — the new room's temperature and humidity reshaping the soundboard — that drifts the tuning, not the motion itself. Let the instrument settle into its new environment for a week or two, then have it tuned. Tuning is a technician's work, not a mover's: we move pianos; we do not tune them, and no tuning arrangement is part of our service.

Do you move museum items?

Yes — museum-item moving is a confirmed service. This category collects the white-glove movement of antiques, art and exhibits, handled piece by piece and custom-crated where needed, with high-mass pieces planned under SIR and the KIM-GS Protocol and discreet scheduling — no client named, ever. Museum institutional terms such as condition reports and courier accompaniment are not claimed.

When does a piece get a custom crate?

Protection is matched to the piece. Furniture and pieces travel fully covered in padded moving blankets and sealed with stretch wrap; a piece that needs more — because of its structure, its journey, or its value — gets a custom crate built around it.

What about a heavy piano, antique or exhibit?

A high-value piece of 1,500 to 3,500 lbs is surveyed and floor-checked under SIR Structural Integrity Relocation and the KIM-GS Protocol, the floor check referencing L/360, before it moves — planned under the same discipline as any SIR move, so placement never becomes an improvisation at the door.

How is this service quoted?

Every job is surveyed in advance and quoted at one flat rate in writing before move day — hourly pricing is available when a client asks for it, and no per-piece price list is published. Name the pieces in the Detailed Project form: the type, the size, and the stairs at both addresses. A video walkthrough works too — film the piece and its route; we never ask you to lift, move or open anything for the camera.

### Who export and logistics is for

Businesses and households shipping high-value items internationally, and freight customers needing container loading and unloading, transloading between truck, container, and warehouse, and final-mile delivery — backed by our warehouse and transload operation with forklift and track loader handling.

### An export job, step by step

Our published chain runs pack · crate · load · transload · final mile under one roof. Worked out in full, an export packing job follows the standard workflow below — the steps are the same ones the service's article describes as the three protection layers: wrap the item, build the crate to ISPM 15 around it, and keep one unbroken chain of custody.

Step | What happens |

1. Survey | The shipment is surveyed and inventoried — what is moving, where it is going, and what the destination's rules require. |

2. Measure & design | Each piece is measured and weighed, and the crate is designed to the piece — its dimensions, weight, fragile points and centre of mass. |

3. Build the crate | The crate is built around the item from compliant, heat-treated, marked wood under ISPM 15 — not a stock box. |

4. Pack, block & brace | The item is packed first — white-glove wrapping for fragile pieces, padding at every contact point — then blocked, braced and cushioned inside the crate so it cannot shift in transit. |

5. Mark & documentation | The IPPC mark goes on the wood packaging, and the shipment's documentation is assembled for the freight leg and the border. |

6. Load & transload | The crated shipment is loaded, and transloaded between truck, container and warehouse where the route calls for it — including Port of Virginia freight flows. |

7. Freight hand-off & final mile | The shipment hands off to the freight leg with its mark visible for inspection, and the final mile at destination is delivered, brought in, placed and verified where the job calls for it. |

### ISPM 15 — how the standard works (domain reference)

The table and definitions below describe the standard itself — ISPM 15, the International Standards for Phytosanitary Measures No. 15, issued by the International Plant Protection Convention — as published in the standard and in the United States program material from USDA APHIS and the American Lumber Standard Committee. They are reference information about the rules every compliant export shipment works to; they are not a statement of any company's certification or program status.

Treatment | Code | What the standard requires |

Heat treatment | HT | The wood core is held at a minimum of 56 °C for at least 30 continuous minutes, throughout the profile of the wood. |

Dielectric heating | DH | The entire profile of the wood, surface included, reaches a minimum of 60 °C for at least 1 continuous minute. |

Methyl bromide fumigation | MB | An approved fumigation schedule. Methyl bromide is restricted or phased out in many jurisdictions and banned in the European Union. |

Scope — what the standard covers
Solid wood packaging material thicker than 6 mm moving in international trade: crates, pallets, boxes, dunnage and blocking.
Debarked wood (DB)
Whatever the treatment, regulated wood packaging must be made from debarked wood. Bark may remain only in small pieces: less than 3 cm wide regardless of length, or wider pieces whose total surface area is under 50 cm².
The IPPC mark
Applied permanently and legibly, preferably on at least two opposite sides of the unit, avoiding red and orange. It carries the IPPC symbol, the two-letter ISO country code, the unique number of the producer or treatment provider assigned under the national plant protection organization (in the United States the mark also carries the accredited agency's logo), and the treatment code — HT, DH or MB; DB may be added where debarking is shown. A correctly marked unit needs no phytosanitary certificate: the mark replaces it.
Exempt material
Manufactured wood — plywood, oriented strand board, particle board, veneer — is exempt, as are barrels for wine and spirits that were heated during manufacture, sawdust, wood shavings and wood wool, and raw wood pieces 6 mm thick or less.
Repair and remanufacture
A repaired unit — up to about one third of its components replaced — must have every replaced component treated and be re-marked, with previous marks obliterated. Beyond that share, the unit counts as remanufactured and is treated and marked as new.
Destination variation
Most trading economies apply ISPM 15, and some add conditions of their own — Australia, for example, requires bark-free material and publishes its import conditions in BICON. The destination's current rules govern the shipment and are checked before it moves.
Why it matters at the border
Non-compliant wood packaging can be delayed, treated at the shipper's cost, or refused at the port. Compliant, treated and marked wood removes that risk before the shipment ever reaches it.

### Export questions, answered

Why does ISPM 15 matter? Because non-compliant crates can be delayed, treated at your cost, or refused — compliant, heat-treated, marked wood built around the item avoids that.

Do you handle the whole chain? Yes — pack, crate, load, transload, and final mile, with no hand-off risk where the job calls for it.

## Custom crating, defined

Custom crating from The Flat Rate Movers is a rigid wooden crate built around one specific item — measured to that piece, fitted to its weight, fragile points and center of mass, with the item wrapped first, then blocked, braced and cushioned inside so it cannot shift in transit.

This hub carries crating on its own. Export packing under ISPM 15 keeps its home on the Export & Crating page, and the two services meet where they should: where a crated shipment crosses a border, the crate is built to the ISPM 15 standard. The company describes that export packing and crating work as built to the standard; it claims no ISPM 15 certification.

## When a crate, and when padding is enough

The decision turns on the piece and the journey, not the price tag. A piece needs a crate when its structure is the fragile part — thin glass, stone tops, delicate carvings and fine finishes fracture under stress padding cannot absorb; when the journey has hand-offs, because freight transferred between vehicles or terminals is handled and stacked at every touch; when the shape defeats padding, because oversized or irregular pieces cannot be anchored with straps and pads alone; when the piece is crossing a border, where the crate's wood itself becomes regulated; or when the piece is going into storage, where months of stacking pressure and contact from other freight act on it directly. Value sharpens every trigger — a piece worth far more than it weighs is the classic case. Padding earns its keep when the threat list is short: a sturdily built piece, surface-level exposure, one crew carrying it once in one truck, and a room — not a warehouse shelf — at the destination. The honest middle exists too: a standard mirror travels in a mirror carton, and medium-value fragile furniture can be double-boxed where a crate is recommended but not required.

## How a crating job runs

1. Name the pieces — tell us the pieces in the Detailed Project form, or use a video walkthrough: film the piece where it stands; we never ask you to lift, move or open anything for the camera.

2. Survey and measure — each piece is surveyed and measured, and the crate is designed around its weight, fragile points and center of mass.

3. Wrap before wood — the item is packed first, with white-glove wrapping for antiques, art, instruments and fragile pieces and padding at every contact point, before any wood is closed around it.

4. Build and fit the interior — inside the crate, the item is blocked, braced and cushioned so it cannot shift in transit.

5. Close, mark and document — the closed crate is documented with the piece, its weight and its handling needs, and joins the move or the export chain — load, transload and final mile under one roof where the job calls for it.

Heavy pieces are planned, not improvised: a piece in the 1,500 to 3,500 lb band is planned under SIR and the KIM-GS Protocol, with the floor check referencing L/360, its crating scoped inside the same written flat-rate job. We do not sell a stock box as a custom crate.

## Crating for export

Crating is the second of the three protection layers the export pages publish: first the item is wrapped, then the crate is built around it, then the whole shipment moves in one unbroken chain — pack, crate, load, transload, final mile. For export, the crate is built to ISPM 15 from compliant, heat-treated, marked wood, so the shipment clears customs instead of being delayed, treated at the shipper's cost, or refused at a port. A crate built in the northern Valley reaches the ocean through the Port of Virginia chain, and the Valley also holds the port's inland terminal, the Virginia Inland Port at Front Royal, where crated freight enters the port system. The full export service — survey, measure and design, build, pack and brace, mark and documentation, load and transload, freight hand-off and final mile — lives on the Export & Crating and International Export Packing & Crating pages linked below.

## Questions, answered

What is custom crating?

Custom crating means a crate built around one item — measured to that piece, not pulled from a stack of stock boxes. Inside, the piece is blocked, braced and cushioned so it cannot move in transit. Packing wraps an item in flexible protection; a crate gives it a rigid shell that freight systems can stack and handle.

When does a piece need a custom crate?

Five triggers settle it, and any one is enough: the structure itself is fragile — thin glass, stone tops, delicate carvings, fine finishes; the journey has hand-offs between vehicles or terminals; the shape defeats padding, because oversized or irregular pieces cannot be anchored with straps and pads alone; the piece is crossing a border; or the piece is going into storage, where stacking pressure and contact from other freight last for months.

When is padding enough?

Padding handles abrasion and minor impact, and nothing more — it cannot carry a load stacked on it, stop a puncture, or fix a piece against a shifting load. When a piece is sturdily built, its exposure is surface-level scratches and scuffs, one crew carries it once in one truck, and the destination is a room rather than a warehouse shelf, blankets and stretch wrap are the complete answer. A standard mirror can travel in a mirror carton; the line is whether a failure would be a scuff or a fracture.

Which pieces does this service crate?

The pieces that need more than padding: antiques, artwork, machinery parts and high-value equipment — and for export work, also pianos, instruments, and medical and sensitive equipment. Each crate is measured, built and fitted to the piece it protects.

Does an export crate play by different rules?

Yes — the wood becomes part of the regulation. ISPM 15, the International Standards for Phytosanitary Measures No. 15, governs solid wood packaging in international trade: the solid wood must be treated and marked, and wood packaging that does not comply can be delayed, treated at the shipper's cost, or refused. Manufactured wood such as plywood and oriented strand board is exempt; a crate's solid-wood frame and skids are not. Our export packing and crating work is built to the ISPM 15 standard from compliant, heat-treated, marked wood. The company claims no ISPM 15 certification.

What is the difference between a crate, a pallet and a skid?

A skid is a base — runners that carry a load and let handling gear underneath. A pallet is a flat deck on the same principle. Neither has walls. A crate is the base plus an enclosure: panels and a lid that turn protection from a platform into a structure, with the interior fitted so the piece cannot shift.

Can a custom crate be reused?

Often, yes — many custom-built crates are reusable, which spreads the build cost across future moves. Whether a crate suits a second journey depends on its construction and the next piece, so reuse is settled when the next job is scoped, not assumed.

How is custom crating quoted?

We publish no per-crate price list. Crating is scoped per job — the piece is surveyed and measured, and the crate designed around its weight, fragile points and center of mass — and quoted inside the one flat rate in writing before move day, hourly pricing is available when a client asks for it.

What about a heavy piece that needs a crate?

Heavy pieces are planned, not improvised. A piece in the 1,500 to 3,500 lb band is planned under SIR Structural Integrity Relocation and the KIM-GS Protocol, with the floor check referencing L/360, and its crating is scoped inside the same written flat-rate job.

## What transloading is

Transloading is the transfer of freight between truck, container and warehouse: a container is unloaded, its freight counted, sorted and restacked, and the load is rebuilt for the inland leg — split by destination through deconsolidation, passed dock to dock through cross-docking, or staged in the warehouse for timed release and final-mile delivery.

In the most common case the shipment changes mode — out of an ocean container and into domestic equipment, typically a 40 ft ocean container's cargo restacked into 53 ft domestic trailers, so the ocean box returns near the port and the domestic trailer carries the inland leg. It gives the shipper control over routing, speed to multiple markets, and capacity use. The words around it, as the industry uses them: unloading (devanning, also called destuffing) is removing cargo from an ocean container at a warehouse, then sorting and staging it for delivery; deconsolidation is breaking a consolidated container apart by destination, purchase order or SKU; cross-docking is freight that never enters storage — it touches the dock floor for hours, not days, then leaves on the outbound leg the same shift. This hub is the company-wide page for the service; the Winchester, Martinsburg and Virginia Inland Port pages below carry it branch by branch and port by port.

## The three operations, on one floor

Deconsolidation — one inbound container is split into many outbound loads, sorted by destination, order or SKU as your paperwork directs, counted and staged. Each split load is built, wrapped and labeled for its onward leg or final-mile delivery. A deconsolidated load may be staged before it moves.

Cross-docking — freight that should not sit does not sit: inbound loads are broken and recombined straight onto outbound trucks, with the warehouse floor as the transfer point and our crew as the labor, and no staging in between.

Transloading — the umbrella operation: freight changes mode or vehicle — container to truck, truck to warehouse, warehouse to final-mile vehicle — with rework where a load needs it: repalletizing, rewrapping, bracing. The full scope also covers warehouse staging for timed distribution, emergency container recovery for shifted, collapsed or refused loads, and commercial freight handling through to white-glove final-mile delivery.

## How a transload runs

1. Receive — the container is received at the warehouse floor from the port chain.

2. Unload — floor-loaded freight is unloaded by hand, piece by piece; palletized freight is pulled and restacked at the container door.

3. Count — freight is counted against the paperwork as it crosses the dock; damaged or shifted loads are reported and reworked on the floor, not passed on.

4. Sort — freight is sorted by destination, order or SKU, as the paperwork directs.

5. Stage — each split is staged for its onward leg — or held staged for timed release. Freight that should not sit does not sit.

6. Build outbound loads — each outbound load is palletized, wrapped and labeled before it leaves the floor.

7. Transload or deliver — loads move onward by transload to truck or container, or by final-mile delivery.

A transload turn is planned as a scheduled operation inside the carrier's free time, because an unplanned queue at the door is where the demurrage and detention clocks start. Empties are turned around instead of sitting.

## Who it is for

This service is for the people who move freight through ports and need the inland link to hold: importers and distributors receiving regular overseas shipments; retail and e-commerce businesses turning stock over fast; 3PLs, freight forwarders and brokers who need a reliable local partner for the warehouse workflow; manufacturers receiving components and raw materials; warehouses and distribution centers facing floor-loaded arrivals, multi-container days, and overflow or surge; and project cargo owners with heavy or oversized loads. The buyer is usually an operations person — a warehouse or logistics manager, a project manager — buying on dock reliability, pace, sequencing and communication.

## The port chain behind the floor

Container freight connected to the Port of Virginia network and the Virginia Inland Port is received at the company's warehouse floor, unloaded or deconsolidated, checked and staged, and built into onward loads for truck dispatch along the I-81, I-66 and I-70 corridors. The Virginia Inland Port at Front Royal, in Warren County, is a Virginia Port Authority intermodal container transfer facility at the I-81 / I-66 junction, with Norfolk Southern containerized rail service five days a week between Front Royal and the Port of Virginia's marine terminals, and U.S. Customs designation as a port of entry. The port's statuses belong to the port: this company is a private handling operation near it — not the Virginia Inland Port, not a customs broker, and operator of no bonded warehouse or foreign-trade zone activity. The Virginia Inland Port page and the guide below carry that chain in depth.

## Questions, answered

What does Loading, Transloading and Container Services include?

Container loading and unloading, and transloading between truck, container and warehouse — counted, sorted and restacked for the inland leg, with cross-docking and warehouse staging.

What is transloading, exactly?

Transloading is the process of moving a shipment from one mode of transport to another — from an ocean container to a truck, in the most common case. The contents of one load unit are unloaded (destuffed) and loaded into another load unit that suits the next leg better. It tends to happen near port terminals or inland satellite terminals — anywhere the freight's vehicle stops being the right vehicle.

How is transloading different from cross-docking and deconsolidation?

Cross-docking means freight never enters storage: it leaves on outbound LTL or FTL the same shift. Deconsolidation means breaking one consolidated container apart by destination, purchase order, or SKU into many outbound loads. A transload often includes one or both, plus storage between legs where needed.

What do free time, demurrage, and detention mean for my shipment?

Free time is the window before charges start; the last free day (LFD) ends it. Past LFD, the terminal charges demurrage for a box sitting at the terminal, and the carrier charges detention (per-diem) for a box kept outside the terminal. Moving the box inside free time — and transloading promptly — is how those charges are avoided.

What if my container is overweight?

Where a container genuinely cannot be permitted to destination, transloading its cargo into domestic trailers removes the container weight from the equation; for some lanes that is cheaper than permitting even when a permit is available. Scope and pricing are quoted per job.

How is transloading priced?

Per job, at one flat rate. We review the full scope — the container, the freight, the sort, any rework, staging and the onward legs — and agree the price in writing before dispatch. There is no per-container rate and no automatic or instant estimate; the estimate is human-made. Guaranteed Flat Rate or Your Move is Free!

Which branch serves my transload — Winchester or Martinsburg?

Winchester transloads are served by The Flat Rate Movers (116 W Piccadilly St Suite 11, Winchester VA 22601; Mon-Fri 8-6, Sat 8-4, Sun 9-4). Martinsburg transloads are served by Flat Rate Movers Martinsburg WV (736 Williamsport Pike Suite 2, Martinsburg WV 25404; Mon-Fri 9-6, Sat 9-4, Sun 9-4) on its own page. Hours and names differ by branch and are listed separately above.

Do you offer bonded warehousing, customs brokerage or FTZ services?

No — and the distinction matters. The Virginia Inland Port is a U.S. Customs-designated port of entry, and its ground in the Warren County Industrial Corridor is covered by Foreign Trade Zone 20 magnet sites (the zone’s grantee is the Virginia Port Authority); Warren County also lies within Foreign Trade Zone 185’s service area, which is not a site designation. Those are the port's statuses, not ours. We are a private handling operation near the port: we do not broker customs, we operate no bonded warehouse and no foreign-trade zone activity, and we claim no refrigerated or cold-chain handling and no hazmat handling. What we do is the physical work — unload, count, split, stage, rework and deliver the freight.

What if the load includes a very heavy item?

If a transload involves a high-mass asset in the 1,500–3,500 lb range, that asset moves under Structural Integrity Relocation (SIR), with floor deflection analysis to L/360, as part of the same flat-rate job. SIR is not claimed for transloading generally; it applies only where such an asset is actually involved.

How do I get a flat rate quote for a transload?

Get My Flat Rate Quote — Short (Quick Quote) by default, or Detailed Project, switching in place with From, To, and What's moving preserved.

FINAL-MILE DELIVERY — WINCHESTER VA & MARTINSBURG WV

# Final-Mile Delivery

## Final-mile delivery, defined

Final-mile delivery is the last leg of a freight journey, from the warehouse or hub to the address where the item belongs. At The Flat Rate Movers it means delivery in, not a drop: the item is carried inside, set in its final position, and verified with the recipient.

## Final-mile delivery, on stated terms

This service is final-mile delivery with in-home or in-business placement and verification — delivered to the room or site where it belongs, placed, and confirmed on site. The chain behind the delivery is the company's own: containers and trucks are unloaded on the company's warehouse floor, freight is counted and inventoried as it crosses the dock, staged, deconsolidated or cross-docked where a shipment needs to split or change vehicles, and reworked where needed — repalletized, rewrapped, braced — then delivered in by the crew that handled it. There is no hand-off to an unknown last carrier. Valuable and fragile freight travels padded in blankets and sealed in stretch wrap — the white-glove wrap standard — with custom crating and ISPM 15 export packing on the same floor for freight that needs it. Deliveries run to homes, offices, industrial sites and retail. A heavy delivery of 1,500 to 3,500 lbs — a safe, a piano, medical equipment — is surveyed and floor-checked to L/360 under SIR Structural Integrity Relocation and the KIM-GS Protocol before it is scheduled. Every job is quoted per job at one flat rate agreed in writing before dispatch; hourly pricing is available when a client asks for it, and no rate schedule for this service is published. Assembly and installation are not part of the published final-mile scope, haul-away of old items is not published as part of the service, and no fixed delivery-window length is published — the appointment is set when the job is scoped.

## Who calls

Retail and e-commerce operations managers whose big-and-bulky products cannot end at a curb. Furniture and appliance retailers whose customers expect the item in the room, not on the driveway. Manufacturers and importers whose freight lands through the Port of Virginia or Virginia Inland Port chain and needs a delivered-in last leg. Third-party logistics and warehouse operators needing a final-mile arm behind their staging. Interior designers receiving pieces that must be placed, not dropped. Facility and office managers receiving equipment and furnishings. Households receiving high-value, fragile or heavy items — a safe, a piano, medical equipment — who need the item placed and verified. If the last fifty feet decide whether the delivery succeeded, this page is written for you.

## The situations

Freight that cannot end at a curb — big-and-bulky, fragile or high-value items whose seller's delivery stops at the driveway. Retail delivery promises — a sale made on placement in the room, which a curbside carrier cannot keep. Port and container freight — a shipment arriving by container or truck for a Shenandoah Valley or Eastern Panhandle address, needing the inland last leg finished properly. Staged freight — freight already on a warehouse floor that needs deconsolidation, cross-docking or rework before it can deliver. Heavy deliveries — an item of 1,500 to 3,500 lbs that needs the SIR survey and L/360 floor check before the delivery is scheduled, not an improvisation at the door. Business receiving — offices, industrial sites and retail spaces receiving equipment and furnishings that must be set in place and verified, not signed for at a dock door.

## How a final-mile delivery runs

One operation runs the whole chain — the freight is never handed to an unknown last carrier. Each step below is the published standard on the combined freight page and in the service's published datasets.

1. Receive and unload — containers and trucks are unloaded on our warehouse floor, and freight is counted and inventoried as it crosses the dock.

2. Stage and rework — freight is staged, deconsolidated or cross-docked where a shipment needs to split or change vehicles, and reworked where needed — repalletized, rewrapped, braced.

3. Protect — valuable and fragile freight travels padded in blankets and sealed in stretch wrap — the white-glove wrap standard — with custom crating and ISPM 15 packing on the same floor for freight that needs it.

4. Deliver in — the item is carried in on a planned route — never left at the curb — to homes, offices, industrial sites and retail.

5. Place — the item is set in its final position, where it belongs.

6. Remove packaging — packaging is removed as agreed, so the recipient is not left with the wrap and the boxes.

7. Verify — placement and condition are verified with the recipient before the crew leaves.

Where a delivery weighs 1,500 to 3,500 lbs, the SIR survey and L/360 floor check join the chain before the delivery is scheduled. For a delivery that needs scoping now, call +1-540-422-2153 — the job is reviewed in full and quoted at one flat rate in writing before dispatch.

## Delivery levels — curbside, threshold, room of choice, white glove

Final-mile delivery is sold in levels, and the level describes one thing: how far the crew carries the item. Curbside ends at the curb, driveway or loading area — the item is left at the edge of the property and everything after that is the recipient's. Threshold ends just inside the first door, garage or lobby — the hardest carry is done; placement is not. Room of choice ends in the room the recipient picks — the item is carried to the room and set down there, with no unpacking. Room of choice with packaging removal adds unpacking and taking the packaging away. White glove is the top of the ladder: room of choice plus unpacking, inspection with the recipient, and packaging and debris removal. Some providers stack assembly or installation above white glove. The names are not standardized anywhere in the industry — no regulator defines them — so the details confirmed in writing are worth more than the level named on a quote. This company's published position on that ladder is plain: the top of the ladder is the standard — delivered in, placed, packaging removed, verified — and the bottom rung is the thing it never does: never left at the curb, never a curbside drop. No lower tier, curbside or threshold-only, is published as an offer.

## Delivery levels, explained — industry background, not our terms

Everything in this section is general industry information, drawn from the sources cited in the Sources card below. It explains how delivery is generally sold and confirmed. It is NOT The Flat Rate Movers' terms: our terms — one operation end to end, delivered in and verified, one flat rate quoted in writing before dispatch — are stated in the sections above.

### Why the same name covers different work

Every seller writes its own definitions. One retailer's published options make its standard delivery threshold for small items but curbside by freight carrier for large ones, with white glove a paid upgrade on both. Industry knowledge bases describe the top tier the same careful way: white-glove delivery "may include" inside placement, assembly, installation and debris removal, and the actual scope "varies by carrier and agreement." Two quotes can both say white glove and deliver different rooms, different unpacking and different debris outcomes. The label is marketing; the confirmed list is the service.

### What to confirm before you book — at any level

The endpoint — curb, first door, or a named room, and if the room is up stairs, whether those flights are included and how many. Unpacking — whether the item is unboxed or uncrated at delivery, or handed over still packaged. Packaging removal, and what it excludes — taking the delivered item's own packaging away is one service; hauling away the old item it replaces is a different one. Assembly and installation — included, excluded, or not offered at all; at the white-glove tier both are "may include" items in the industry's own descriptions, so assume nothing. The appointment — whether there is a scheduled appointment, who has to be present, and whether a signature is required. Inspection at signing — inspect the item in place and record its condition before the delivery paperwork is signed; federal consumer guidance for household-goods moves turns on the same habit. The failed-delivery answer — if the item cannot be carried in, what happens next, and who pays for the second attempt.

### Why the top tier costs more

The top tier buys labor and time, not a label: two-person teams instead of a driver alone, a scheduled appointment instead of a route stop, the minutes to carry, place, unpack and inspect, and the liability management of handling heavy, fragile or high-value freight inside a home or business. Curbside is cheaper because everything after the curb — the carry, the placement, the unpacking, the risk on the stairs — transfers to the recipient.

## Questions, answered

What is final-mile delivery, exactly?

The final mile is the last leg of a freight journey: from the last facility — a port terminal, a warehouse, a regional hub — to the address where the item belongs. It is the only leg of the journey the recipient watches happen, and it is where a shipment that has traveled thousands of miles can still fail in the last fifty feet. In our operation the chain is unbroken: freight is unloaded on our own warehouse floor, counted and inventoried as it crosses the dock, staged or deconsolidated, then delivered in by the same operation — no hand-off to an unknown last carrier.

What does Final-Mile Delivery include?

Final-mile delivery with in-home or in-business placement and verification. The published chain: freight is received and unloaded on our warehouse floor and counted as it crosses the dock; staged, deconsolidated or cross-docked, and reworked where needed; protected under the white-glove wrap standard; then delivered in on a planned route, set in its final position, its packaging removed as agreed, and its placement and condition verified with the recipient before the crew leaves.

Who is Final-Mile Delivery for?

Households and businesses needing final-mile delivery with in-home or in-business placement and verification — retail and e-commerce operations whose big-and-bulky products cannot end at a curb, retailers whose customers expect the item in the room, manufacturers and importers landing freight through the Port of Virginia or Virginia Inland Port chain, designers, facility managers, and households receiving high-value, fragile or heavy items.

Will my delivery be left at the curb?

No. The published standard is the top of the delivery ladder: the item crosses the threshold, is set in its final position, its packaging is removed as agreed, and placement is verified with the recipient. Curbside and threshold-only tiers are not published as offers — the published standard starts inside the door.

What are the delivery levels?

Curbside (left at the curb or driveway); threshold (carried inside the first door, garage or lobby); room of choice (carried to the room the recipient picks, no unpacking); room of choice with packaging removal; and white glove (room of choice plus unpacking, inspection with the recipient, and packaging and debris removal). Some providers add assembly or installation at the top tier. The ladder is industry vocabulary — no regulator defines these names — which is why the confirmation list matters more than the label on the quote.

What should you confirm before you book?

Confirm in writing, whichever level you are buying: the endpoint (curb, first door, or a named room — and whether stairs are included); unpacking; packaging removal and what it excludes; assembly and installation; the appointment, who must be present, and whether a signature is required; inspection at signing, with condition recorded before the paperwork is signed; and the failed-delivery answer — what happens, and who pays, if the item cannot be carried in.

Can a final-mile delivery be scheduled?

Yes — appointment-based delivery is the norm for freight of any size, and our deliveries are arranged by appointment too. No fixed window length is published for this service — the appointment is set when the job is scoped and quoted.

Is final-mile delivery available for residences?

Yes. Our final-mile deliveries run to homes as well as to offices, industrial sites and retail spaces, dispatched from the Winchester and Martinsburg branches. A residence with stairs or a heavy piece is exactly the delivery to confirm in detail before the day.

Why does white-glove delivery cost more than curbside?

Because the service is different work, not a different label. The top tier carries two-person teams, the scheduling coordination of an appointment, the extra time to carry, place, unpack and inspect, and the liability management of handling heavy or high-value freight inside the building. A curbside price stops at the curb — and hands you the carry, the placement and the stair risk.

What should I check before I sign for a delivery?

Check the item in its final position before the paperwork is signed: finish, corners, doors and drawers, and whether it is complete. Note any damage on the delivery documents, not after the crew has gone. Our crews verify condition with you before they leave.

Does final-mile delivery include assembly?

Sometimes in the industry — and only when it is agreed. Industry descriptions list assembly among the things white-glove service may include, and the scope depends on the carrier and the agreement, so it has to be confirmed before booking. On our side the answer is plain: assembly and installation are not part of our published final-mile scope. If a delivery turns on either, settle it with us when the job is scoped.

Is debris removal included with a delivery?

Removing the delivered item's own packaging is one service; hauling away the old item it replaces is another, and the second is not implied by the first. Our published practice covers the delivered item's packaging — removed as agreed. Haul-away of old items is not published as part of our service.

## White-glove delivery, defined

## White-glove delivery, on stated terms

White-glove delivery means the item crosses the threshold: brought in on a planned route, set in its final position, packaging removed and condition verified with you before the crew leaves — never left at a curb. It is the delivery end of the company's white-glove standard, which the service registry states for pianos, antiques and high-value items: surveyed, protected, and moved with custom crating when the piece requires it, at one flat rate agreed in writing. The work runs piece by piece, never bulk: each piece is assessed on its own — weight, fragile points, finish and value at risk — then wrapped, padded or crated to match. Furniture and pieces travel fully covered in padded blankets and sealed with clear stretch wrap; pieces that need more get a custom crate built around them. Antiques, art, pianos and instruments are the everyday work of this service. Behind the delivery sits the same freight floor as the company's final-mile chain: freight is received and counted on the warehouse floor, staged, deconsolidated or cross-docked, and reworked where needed, then delivered in by the crew that handled it — no hand-off to an unknown last carrier. A high-value delivery that weighs 1,500 to 3,500 lbs — a safe, a piano, medical equipment — is surveyed and floor-checked to L/360 under SIR Structural Integrity Relocation and the KIM-GS Protocol before it is scheduled, so placement never becomes an improvisation at the door. Every job is quoted at one flat rate agreed in writing before dispatch; hourly pricing is available when a client asks for it, and no rate schedule for this service is published. Assembly and installation are not part of the published scope, and haul-away of old items is not published as part of the service.

## Who calls

Winchester and Panhandle clients receiving high-value, fragile or heavy items who need white-glove delivery, not a curbside drop. Collectors, estates and high-value households receiving pieces that cannot be replaced. Retailers and designers whose delivery promise includes placement in the room. ## The situations

High-value and fragile pieces — antiques, art, pianos and instruments, assessed piece by piece and protected to match. A purchase whose seller stops at the curb — the item still has to cross the threshold, climb the stairs and land in its room. Heavy deliveries — a safe, a piano or medical equipment of 1,500 to 3,500 lbs, surveyed and floor-checked to L/360 before the delivery is scheduled. Retail and designer receiving — pieces that must be placed, unpacked and inspected with the recipient, with the packaging taken away. Pieces that need more than padding — a custom crate built around the piece when blankets and stretch wrap are not enough, with ISPM 15 export packing on the same floor when the journey crosses a border.

## How a white-glove delivery runs

1. Name the pieces — the client names the pieces; each piece is assessed on its own — weight, fragile points, finish and value at risk.

2. Match the protection — padded blankets and clear stretch wrap as the standard, a custom crate built around the piece when it needs more; high-mass pieces are surveyed and floor-checked to L/360 under SIR and the KIM-GS Protocol before they move.

3. Receive and stage — freight arriving through the freight chain is unloaded on the warehouse floor, counted and inventoried as it crosses the dock, and staged for the delivery.

4. Deliver in on a planned route — the item crosses the threshold on a planned route — never left at a curb — to homes, offices, industrial sites and retail.

5. Place — the item is set in its final position, where it belongs.

6. Remove packaging — the delivered item's packaging is removed, so the recipient is not left with the wrap and the boxes.

7. Verify — placement and condition are verified with the recipient before the crew leaves.

For a delivery that needs scoping now, call +1-540-422-2153 — the job is reviewed in full and quoted at one flat rate in writing before dispatch.

## Delivery levels — where white glove sits

Final-mile delivery is sold in levels, and the level describes one thing: how far the crew carries the item. Curbside — the item is left at the curb or driveway; under this page's published standard, never a curbside drop. Threshold — the item is carried inside the first door, garage or lobby, no further. Room of choice — the item is carried to the room the recipient picks; unpacking is not included. Room of choice with packaging removal — placement in the room, and the packaging is taken away. White glove — this service — brought in on a planned route, set in its final position, packaging removed, and condition verified with the recipient before the crew leaves. Some providers stack assembly or installation above white glove. The ladder is the industry's vocabulary, published here as a reference — the last row is where this company's published standard sits. The names are not standardized anywhere in the industry, so the details confirmed in writing are worth more than the level named on a quote.

## Delivery levels, explained — industry background, not our terms

Everything in this section is general industry information, drawn from the sources cited in the Sources card below. It explains how delivery is generally sold and confirmed. It is NOT The Flat Rate Movers' terms: our terms — placed, unpacked and verified as the standard, one flat rate quoted in writing before dispatch — are stated in the sections above.

### Why the same name covers different work

Every seller writes its own definitions. One retailer's published options make its standard delivery threshold for small items but curbside by freight carrier for large ones, with white glove a paid upgrade on both. Industry knowledge bases describe the top tier the same careful way: white-glove delivery "may include" inside placement, assembly, installation and debris removal, and the actual scope "varies by carrier and agreement." Two quotes can both say white glove and deliver different rooms, different unpacking and different debris outcomes. The label is marketing; the confirmed list is the service.

### What to confirm before you book — at any level

The endpoint — curb, first door, or a named room, and if the room is up stairs, whether those flights are included and how many. Unpacking — whether the item is unboxed or uncrated at delivery, or handed over still packaged. Packaging removal, and what it excludes — taking the delivered item's own packaging away is one service; hauling away the old item it replaces is a different one. Assembly and installation — included, excluded, or not offered at all; at the white-glove tier both are "may include" items in the industry's own descriptions, so assume nothing. The appointment — whether there is a scheduled appointment, who has to be present, and whether a signature is required. Inspection at signing — inspect the item in place and record its condition before the delivery paperwork is signed; federal consumer guidance for household-goods moves turns on the same habit. The failed-delivery answer — if the item cannot be carried in, what happens next, and who pays for the second attempt.

### Why the top tier costs more

The top tier buys labor and time, not a label: two-person teams instead of a driver alone, a scheduled appointment instead of a route stop, the minutes to carry, place, unpack and inspect, and the liability management of handling heavy, fragile or high-value freight inside a home or business. Curbside is cheaper because everything after the curb — the carry, the placement, the unpacking, the risk on the stairs — transfers to the recipient.

## The account side of white glove: receiving, holding, and the install day

Half of this service happens before a customer ever sees a truck. Brands, retailers, and designers ship pieces ahead to us; we receive them, inspect each piece on arrival, issue a receiving inspection report, photograph its condition, and hold it in storage until the install day. Freight damage is documented while the carrier can still answer for it — when a piece comes off a carrier terminal instead, the crew notes any carton damage on the carrier's own ticket before signing and sends photographs to the account immediately.

On the day, the crew delivers to the room the piece was bought for: full assembly — the complete build, with appliance hookups completed where the job includes appliances — the replaced item hauled away, packaging and pallets out, and photographs at three stages, arrival, unboxed, and placed, so the customer, the brand, and the carrier share one condition record. Stairs run any number of flights, up or down. Inside our home territory our own crews deliver; a job beyond it is fulfilled by a vetted partner we coordinate, under the same written scope. Every job is quoted per job, in writing, before work begins.
