## Questions, answered

What is freight rework?

Freight rework is the corrective handling that returns a load to a deliverable state: freight that shifted in transit, a load a receiver refused at the dock, damaged or collapsed pallets, and overweight or axle-illegal loads are unloaded under control, sorted, restacked, repalletized, re-wrapped and re-secured — with the damage separated and documented — so the truck can deliver or legally roll. The Flat Rate Movers performs freight reworks and load-shift corrections from Winchester, VA and Martinsburg, WV, at the company's leased space, the receiver's dock, or a yard — wherever the job requires.

My load shifted on the road. What happens now?

Call +1-540-422-2153. Intake records what happened, where the truck is and what the freight is — photos of the load as it sits speed the quote. The job is scoped and quoted at one flat rate before work begins. At the site, the trailer is opened under control because a shifted load can fall at the doors; the load is photographed as found, counted against the bill of lading, unloaded in sequence, restacked and repalletized, reloaded in delivery sequence, and secured so the tiedowns' aggregate working load limit reaches at least half the cargo weight, the federal standard in 49 CFR 393.106(d). You leave with after-photos, final counts and bill-of-lading notation of the work.

A receiver refused my load. Can you rebuild it for redelivery?

Yes. Refused and rejected loads are a core part of this service: leaning or collapsed pallets are rebuilt, freight is restacked to the receiver's Ti/Hi pattern and stack height, mixed product is sorted to specification, damaged cases are pulled and documented, and counts are verified against the bill of lading. The rebuilt load is photographed and signed for at hand-back, so the redelivery arrives as documented.

Can you correct an overweight or axle-weight problem?

Yes. Axle correction is part of the rework scope: freight is repositioned along the box, redistributed between the steer, drive and tandem axles, partially offloaded and reloaded, or split across equipment, so the truck can legally roll — verified against the scale ticket where a scale is part of the job.

Do you repalletize freight to a receiver's specification?

Yes. Rebuilding to the receiver's specification is the point of the work: sound pallets of the required type, the receiver's Ti/Hi pattern and stack height, failed packaging replaced where needed, and the load re-wrapped and secured. Floor-loaded freight is also palletized to specification for receivers that accept palletized freight only.

What documentation comes with a rework?

Photographs of the load as found before it is touched, counts against the bill of lading at unload and at reload, specific damage exceptions written on the delivery paperwork, after-photos of the rebuilt load, bill-of-lading notation of the work performed, and receiver or carrier sign-off at hand-back. The record is built to support the OS&D report and any cargo claim that follows — a clean signature with unnoted damage is the carrier's best evidence against a claim, so exceptions are written at the dock, while the driver is present.

How is a freight rework quoted?

Every job is scoped in full — the freight, the situation, the location, the manpower and the handling the job requires — and quoted at one flat rate before work begins. Nothing is auto-priced and hourly pricing is available when a client asks for it. Photos of the load as it sits speed the intake. Emergency and after-hours work is quoted at the emergency premium. No rate card for this service is published; the price for a job is the flat rate quoted for that job.

Is emergency or after-hours rework available?

Yes. Emergency and after-hours response for shifted, refused and axle-held loads is available, at premium rates. A load standing still is burning detention and a driver's hours; call +1-540-422-2153 and the intake starts with where the truck is and what the freight is.

What is the difference between cross-docking, transloading and rework?

Rework fixes the freight: the load cannot deliver as it sits, and the corrective work returns it to a deliverable, legal, secured state. Cross-docking moves the freight: inbound freight is unloaded and transferred directly onto outbound vehicles, sorted and consolidated dock to dock, typically turned in under 24 hours with little to no storage — best for high-velocity goods, retail distribution, e-commerce and perishables. Transloading changes the mode: freight moves between transportation modes — ocean container or railcar to domestic truck — and may be repalletized, sorted or held in short staging during the switch — best for long-distance international shipping, intermodal networks and bulk or heavy goods. A rework can be inserted into either operation when freight arrives wrong.

Do you perform rail-to-truck transloading?

The company works rail-served spots when contracted: at a rail-served location, the transfer chain runs railcar arrival and inbound checks, unload, staging or sorting in the transfer area, and outbound truck loads built for the delivery leg, with counts taken at every touch so the inventory record survives the mode change. The company claims no owned rail siding or railroad authority; the work is contracted transfer work at the facility's location.

Where does the rework happen?

Wherever the job requires: the company's leased space, the receiver's dock, or a yard. Dispatch runs from both branches — The Flat Rate Movers in Winchester, VA and Flat Rate Movers Martinsburg WV — across the I-81, I-66 and I-70 corridors; the two branches are distinct, with their own addresses, hours and service areas.

Who pays for unloading and rework labor?

Under federal law, the shipper or receiver is financially responsible for loading and unloading assistance — 49 USC 14103 — not the driver; a driver who pays at the dock is reimbursed on the receipt, and the lumper fees charged at receivers typically run per load. The rework itself is quoted by this company at one flat rate before work begins; who ultimately bears that cost between shipper, carrier, broker and receiver is a matter for their contracts and any cargo claim.

Can floor-loaded freight be palletized?

Yes. Floor-loaded containers and trailers are unloaded piece by piece, counted and checked, and built onto pallets to the receiver's specification — the standard inland leg for container freight moving through the Virginia Inland Port chain and for imports that arrive floor-loaded.

Do you handle damaged freight?

Yes. Damaged freight is separated from good freight at the unload — crushed, torn or water-damaged cases are pulled, photographed and documented, never buried back into the load — so the deliverable part of the shipment can still deliver, and the damaged part carries the documentation an OS&D report and a cargo claim require.

## What this service is — and what it is not

Logistics project management, as this company sells it, is the planning and accountable execution of a defined piece of logistics work: a container devanning program at a port-adjacent warehouse, a distribution-center load-out, a warehouse reset or re-slot, a racking or FF&E support project, a freight-rework campaign, a surge that needs a crew plan instead of a hope. The deliverable is the finished piece of work, run to a plan we wrote and stand behind — not advice, not a staffing requisition, and not a software dashboard.

It is deliberately scoped. This is not generic logistics consulting, not freight brokerage, not transportation management, and not a claim to run anyone's supply chain. The company does not run port drayage — freight moves to and from the ports and sites on the customer's or the carrier's trucks — and it holds no tenancy at any terminal and claims no port-authority relationship. What it brings to a project is the layer that is usually missing between the plan on paper and the freight on the floor: a surveyed scope, a crew sized to the work, a sequence that respects doors, docks and deadlines, supervised execution, and a closeout that says exactly what was done.

The service exists because of where this company already works. The same crews that transload at the Virginia Inland Port, unload containers around Norfolk Harbor, and rework freight at receivers' docks across two states kept being asked the same question by operations managers: can you just run the whole piece? This service is that answer, registered as its own category so the accountability is explicit: one plan, one lead, one flat rate.

## How a project runs — the five stages

### 1. Survey

Every project starts with a survey of the actual work: the site and its access, the freight or the building, volumes and unit shapes where they are known, the delivery points, the dates and the hard deadlines inside them. For container work the survey covers what is arriving, in what condition it is expected, and where it has to end up; for building work it covers the floor, the doors, the dock equipment situation as found, and the sequence constraints the site imposes. The survey is where problems are cheap. A shifted load, a short dock, a barge window at Richmond, a rail cutoff at Front Royal — all of it is priced and planned here, not discovered at dispatch.

### 2. Scope and the flat-rate quote

The survey becomes a written scope: the work, in order, with the crew size, the supervision, the delivery points and the completion definition — what "done" means, in countable terms. The scope is priced at one flat rate, agreed before dispatch. Flat rate is this company's standard offer and its guarantee; if a client prefers hourly pricing for a defined engagement, it is available when they ask. What never happens is a clock discovered after the fact or a scope that quietly grows: if the work on the ground differs from the surveyed work, that is a conversation before it is a charge.

### 3. Crew and sequence plan

With the scope set, the plan fixes the crew — how many hands, which skills, what supervision ratio — and the sequence: what happens first, what waits on what, where freight or material stages between steps, and how the site keeps operating around the work where it must. Port projects are planned against the port's own rhythm: gate hours, barge and rail windows, and the corridor drive from the bound branch. Warehouse projects are planned against the building's rhythm: receiving hours, outbound cutoffs, and the operation that cannot stop while the project runs inside it.

### 4. Execution

Our own supervised crews do the hands-on work — unloading and devanning containers, counting and checking freight at the door, deconsolidating by destination, order or SKU, cross-docking straight-through freight, restacking and rebuilding loads, resetting warehouse space, supporting racking and FF&E work — at port-adjacent warehouses, receivers' docks, yards and leased space. Work on a terminal itself happens only by arrangement, through the terminal's own processes. The project lead runs the plan on site, tracks count against scope, and is the single point of contact for the client's operations team while the work is live.

### 5. Closeout

The project closes against its scope: what was received, what was done to it, where it went, and anything that arrived damaged, short or different from its paperwork — recorded at the door, not reconstructed later. The closeout is the document the client's team files: counts, condition notes and the completion state, tied back to the scope line by line. A project is done when the closeout says it is done, and the flat rate was the flat rate.

## The projects this service runs

### Container programs

Recurring or one-off container work planned as a program instead of a scramble: devanning waves as boxes land, deconsolidation by destination or SKU, restacking and palletizing to the receiver's standard, and load-out to the outbound leg — at the warehouses, docks and yards around the six ports, and at Valley distribution buildings fed by the Virginia Inland Port's rail ramps.

### Warehouse load-outs, resets and re-slots

Defined building projects with a completion state: full or partial load-outs, layout resets, re-slotting programs, seasonal changeovers, and the labor-heavy middle of a warehouse relocation where the building's own team cannot be in two places at once.

### Surge and deadline programs

Peak-season surges, promotional waves, a carrier's backlog, a barge or rail bunching event — work whose defining feature is a date. The project plan sizes the crew to the date and sequences the work so the deadline is met by arithmetic, not optimism.

### Freight-rework campaigns

When one shifted load is a bad day but a pattern of them is a project: rework campaigns for receivers and carriers — collapsed pallets rebuilt, mixed freight separated, damaged cases culled and recorded — run as a scoped program with per-unit closeout counts, at the receiver's dock, a yard, or leased space.

### Racking, FF&E and in-plant support projects

The project layer over the company's industrial work: racking relocation support, FF&E installation programs, and office-inside-a-plant moves, where the sequence — what comes down, what moves, what goes back, in what order — is the difference between a project and a pile.

### Port-adjacent staging projects

Project cargo and breakbulk support around the terminals: staging, sorting, crating coordination and load support for the heavy and out-of-gauge freight that moves through Newport News and Portsmouth Marine Terminal's heavy-lift berths, and the reefer and perishable programs at Philadelphia and Wilmington where the cargo's clock runs fastest.

## Where it runs — the six ports and the Valley

Port project work binds to the branch the port is bound to, by measured road distance: the Virginia Inland Port at Front Royal (about 23 miles from Winchester), the Port of Virginia at Norfolk (about 222 miles from Winchester) and Richmond Marine Terminal (about 135 miles from Winchester) are Winchester projects; the Port of Baltimore (about 91–96 miles from Martinsburg), the Port of Wilmington, Delaware (about 150 miles from Martinsburg) and PhilaPort (about 191 miles from Martinsburg, bound on drive time — the road miles are tied, and no mileage advantage is claimed) are Martinsburg projects. The full binding map, with both branches' distances for every port, is published on the program hub at /port-logistics/ and in the ports dataset.

Inland, the service covers the distribution geography the ports feed: the Front Royal and Winchester warehouse cluster on the I-81/I-66 junction, the Martinsburg logistics buildings on the I-81/I-70 corridor, and the port-adjacent warehouse clusters around Hampton Roads, Richmond, Baltimore, Wilmington and Philadelphia — always at the client's site, the receiver's dock, a yard or leased space, under the delivery-point rule that governs all of this company's port work.

## How it joins the rest of the crew layer

Project management is the planning and accountability layer; the hands are the company's standing services. A managed project draws on specialized workforce labor (#/specialized-workforce-labor) for its crews, transloading and container services (#/transloading) for the freight handling itself, freight rework (#/freight-rework-transloading) when loads arrive wrong, cross-docking (#/cross-docking-services) when freight should cross the dock instead of entering storage, and 3PL support services (#/3pl-support-services) when the project runs inside a 3PL's or a distribution center's operation. The client buys one accountable piece of work; which of those services the plan draws on is our problem, sequenced in the scope — not a set of separate engagements to coordinate.

## Questions, answered

What is logistics project management, in this company's service?
It is the planning and accountable execution of a defined piece of port, warehouse or industrial logistics work: we survey the work, scope it in full, build the crew and sequence plan, run it with our own supervised crews, and close it out against the scope. The deliverable is the finished piece of work at one flat rate — not consulting, not staffing, and not transportation management.

What kinds of projects do you manage?
Container programs (devanning, deconsolidation, restacking and load-out), warehouse load-outs, resets and re-slots, surge and deadline programs, freight-rework campaigns, racking and FF&E support projects, office-inside-a-plant moves, and port-adjacent staging projects for breakbulk and project cargo — at port-adjacent warehouses, receivers' docks, yards and leased space around the six ports we serve and across the Shenandoah Valley and Eastern Panhandle.

How does a project start?
With a survey of the actual work — the site, the freight or the building, the delivery points, the dates and the deadlines inside them. The survey becomes a written scope with a completion definition in countable terms, priced at one flat rate agreed before dispatch. Problems are found at the survey, where they are cheap, not at dispatch.

Who is accountable while the work is running?
Our project lead, on site, as the single point of contact for your operations team. The lead runs the crew and sequence plan, tracks count against scope, and owns the closeout: what was received, what was done, where it went, and anything that arrived damaged, short or different from its paperwork — recorded at the door.

Do you manage transportation or run drayage for a project?
No. Drayage and linehaul are not part of this service, or of any service this company sells. Freight moves to and from ports and sites on your trucks or your carrier's trucks; our project work is the planning, the crews and the hands-on execution where the freight is received, staged and handed on.

Which ports does the service cover, and which branch runs them?
Six ports, each bound to one branch by measured road distance. Winchester runs the Virginia Inland Port (about 23 miles), the Port of Virginia at Norfolk (about 222 miles) and Richmond Marine Terminal (about 135 miles). Martinsburg runs the Port of Baltimore (about 91–96 miles), the Port of Wilmington (about 150 miles) and PhilaPort (about 191 miles, bound on drive time — the road miles are tied). The full binding map is published on the port logistics hub and in the ports dataset.

How is project work priced?
Every engagement is surveyed and scoped in full — scope, distance, manpower and equipment reviewed — and quoted at one flat rate agreed before dispatch. Flat rate is the company's standard offer and its guarantee: Guaranteed Flat Rate or Your Move is Free! If a client prefers hourly pricing for a defined engagement, it is available when they ask for it. Port and project pages carry no published rate schedules; each project is quoted on its own scope.

Are your crews credentialed for port work?
Our crews hold TWIC cards and our contractors hold valid TWIC cards. That is card-holding by the people doing the work. The company holds no tenancy at any terminal and claims no port-authority relationship; it serves the ports from its branches via the corridors.

### 3PL Support Services

3PL support services: supervised crews that support operations run by 3PLs, distribution centers and carriers — receiving support, sort and segregation, container crews, freight rework, surge labor and project support. Support, not operator: the company holds no warehouse network, leases no warehouse space for clients and takes no custody of client freight as an operator.

3PL SUPPORT SERVICES · CREWS FOR 3PLS, DCS & CARRIERS

# 3PL Support Services — project crews that support your operation, not replace it

Third-party logistics operations run on labor that flexes: a container program lands early, a client's peak arrives all at once, a new building needs hands before it needs headcount. Our 3PL support services supply that flex — supervised crews for receiving, sorting and segregation, container work, rework and surge labor, inside operations that 3PLs, distribution centers and carriers run themselves.

To be exact about what this is: we are a support service, not a 3PL operator. We do not run a warehouse network, we do not lease warehouse space for clients, and freight in a supported operation stays in the operator's custody, on the operator's systems, under the operator's name. What we bring is the crew layer — trained, supervised, project-managed labor — run from our Winchester and Martinsburg branches to the ports and warehouse corridors both serve. Every engagement is surveyed and scoped in full, then quoted at one flat rate — our standard offer and our guarantee; hourly pricing is available when a client asks for it.

## The line this service holds: support, not operation

A 3PL operator takes custody of a client's freight, warehouses it in space the operator controls, runs it on the operator's systems, and answers for the inventory. This company does none of that under this service, and this page will not pretend otherwise. 3PL support services are the work around that operation, done for the operator: the crews that unload the containers the operation receives, sort and segregate what came out of them, rebuild the loads that arrived wrong, staff the surge the operation did not forecast, and execute the project work — resets, stand-ups, changeovers — that an operation's own headcount cannot absorb without breaking its daily rhythm.

The distinction matters commercially, not just legally. An operator hiring support keeps its client relationships, its systems, its space and its name on the work. Nothing here competes with the operator's offer: we hold no warehouse network to sell, quote no storage under this service, and sign no freight as its custodian. The company's separate moving-and-storage service is a household and commercial storage offer with its own terms; it is not a 3PL warehousing product and is never presented as one. This service is labor and project execution, delivered inside someone else's well-run operation — and priced, scoped and supervised like the project work it is.

That framing is also why the work is supervised, not temped. A staffing agency fills slots; a support crew arrives with a lead, a scope, a sequence and a closeout count. The operations this service supports — 3PL sites, distribution centers, carriers' terminals and receivers' docks from Hampton Roads to Philadelphia — run on numbers: doors turned, units counted, cutoffs met. Support that cannot be counted against a scope is not support. Every engagement here carries the same discipline as the company's project work: surveyed in full, scoped in writing, one flat rate, closed out line by line.

## The support work, task by task

### Receiving support

Crews at the inbound door: unloading containers and trailers, devanning floor-loaded freight, counting and checking against the paperwork at the door, and recording damage, shortage and discrepancy where it is found — at the moment it can still be acted on. Receiving support is where a supported operation gains or loses its inventory accuracy; the count is the product.

### Sort and segregation

Deconsolidation and sort work inside the operation's own rules: freight separated by destination, order, SKU, store, route or disposition, restacked and palletized to the standard the next leg expects. Mixed containers become clean, labeled, countable units that the operator's systems can receive without a second touch.

### Container crews

The container program layer: stuffing and destuffing, packing and unpacking ocean containers to the CTU discipline this company's export work already follows, blocking and bracing coordination, and the load-out work that turns a sorted floor back into sealed boxes on schedule — at port-adjacent warehouses, docks, yards and leased space around the six ports.

### Rework

Support for the freight that arrives wrong: collapsed pallets rebuilt, shifted loads corrected, damaged cases culled and recorded, mixed freight separated. Rework crews run under the operation's disposition rules and report per-unit counts — the difference between a rework pile and a rework program.

### Surge and peak labor

The flex layer for the dates an operation cannot staff to: peak season, promotional waves, a port bunching event, a client's inventory build. Surge engagements are surveyed and scoped like any project — crew size set by the volume and the date, supervised on site, closed out against the scope — not a day-labor call.

### Project support inside live operations

Stand-up labor for new sites and new client onboardings, warehouse resets and re-slots, layout changeovers, inventory-project support and load-outs — the defined pieces of project work that land on an operation mid-quarter. These run under the company's logistics project management (#/logistics-project-management) discipline when the operator wants the whole piece owned, or as scoped crew support under the operator's own project lead when it does not.

## Who buys it, and how the work is directed

The buyers are the people who run operations: 3PL site and operations managers, distribution-center managers, carrier terminal managers, and the receivers whose docks absorb the freight. Day to day, direction follows the operation: the operator's team sets the priorities, the systems and the standards — it is their building, their WMS, their client. Our lead runs our crews against the agreed scope inside that direction, owns the count and the closeout, and is the single point of contact for crew questions. If the scope and the floor disagree, that surfaces through the lead immediately, not at invoicing.

The model extends the one this company's workforce service already runs for warehouses and project sites — trained, supervised teams deployed per job, with no required contract duration — into the specific shape 3PL and DC operations need: door work, sort work, container work and surge work, at the ports those operations draw from and the inland buildings they feed.

## Where support runs — ports and buildings

Support work binds to the branch each port is bound to, by measured road distance. Winchester crews support the operations fed by the Virginia Inland Port (about 23 miles — including the Front Royal distribution cluster the port serves), the Port of Virginia at Norfolk (about 222 miles) and Richmond Marine Terminal (about 135 miles, dataset-level coverage). Martinsburg crews support the Port of Baltimore (about 91–96 miles), the Port of Wilmington (about 150 miles, dataset-level coverage) and PhilaPort (about 191 miles, bound on drive time — the road miles are tied and no mileage advantage is claimed), where the perishable and breakbulk support spoke carries this service. Inland, support runs across the two branches' own warehouse geography: the Winchester and Front Royal buildings on I-81/I-66, and the Martinsburg logistics cluster on the I-81/I-70 corridor. The full coverage matrix — every port, every service, its treatment — is published in the ports dataset.

Everywhere, the delivery-point rule holds: support crews work at the operator's site, a port-adjacent warehouse, a receiver's dock, a yard or leased space. Work on a terminal itself happens only by arrangement, through the terminal's own processes. And the freight that support crews handle arrives and leaves on the operator's, the customer's or the carrier's trucks — this company does not run port drayage under this service or any other.

## The support engagement, step by step

### Survey and scope

A support engagement starts the same way every engagement here does: a survey of the operation's actual gap — the doors, the freight profile, the systems the crew will work inside, the standards the operator holds its own teams to — and a written scope that names the tasks, the crew size, the supervision and the count the closeout will report. The operator sees exactly what is being bought before anything is dispatched.

### Stand-up

Crews are briefed on the site's rules before the first shift: safety, systems, scan discipline, disposition authority — what our hands may decide and what is always the operator's call. The lead walks the floor with the operator's team so the first container is a procedure, not an introduction.

### The run

During the engagement the lead reports against the scope daily: doors turned, units received and sorted, rework counts, exceptions found at the door. If volume outruns the scoped crew — the surge inside the surge — that is raised while adding hands still helps, with the scope amendment priced before it is worked, not after.

### Closeout and handback

The engagement closes with the counts tied to the scope and the work area handed back clean: no partial sorts left ambiguous, no exception freight unrecorded. Operations that run support repeatedly build a standing pattern with us — the same lead, the same brief, the site's rules already known — which is where support stops being a transaction and becomes capacity the operator can plan against.

## Questions, answered

What are 3PL support services?
They are the labor and project layer that supports a third-party logistics operation from outside its own headcount: supervised crews for receiving, sorting and segregation, container stuffing and destuffing, rework, surge coverage and project work — surveyed, scoped, quoted at one flat rate and closed out against the scope, inside an operation the 3PL, distribution center or carrier runs itself.

It supports 3PLs and the operations they run — with crews and project execution — while the operator keeps the space, the systems, the custody and the client relationship.

Receiving support (unloading, devanning, counting and checking at the door, recording damage and shortage), sort and segregation by destination, order, SKU, store or route, container packing and unpacking, freight rework under the operation's disposition rules, surge and peak coverage, and project support — stand-ups, resets, re-slots, changeovers and load-outs. ### Vault Door Relocation & Installation

Vault doors and high-security enclosures delivered, relocated, and installed at any size, quoted at one flat rate agreed in writing before the job — specified from the door's own standards (UL 608, GSA Class 5 under AA-D-600D) and its verified weight, with SIR structural analysis in band and contents emptied first.

Primary page: https://theflatratemovers.com/vault-doors/

# Vault Door Relocation & Installation

Vault doors and high-security enclosures — delivered, relocated, and installed at any size, quoted at one flat rate in writing before the job. The door is planned from its own facts: its standard, its verified weight, its lock, its clear opening, and the floor it will stand on.

Get My Flat Rate Quote (#/quote)

## What we do

Vault door delivery & placement. A door bought from a manufacturer or dealer still has to travel the last stretch — off the truck, through the building, and into the room where it will live. We receive, move, and place vault doors of every class, planned from the door’s stated weight and dimensions, with the route surveyed before the door moves.

Vault door installation — any size. Installation is offered at any size: a residential safe-room door, a bank’s Class 5-V, a modular vault assembled panel by panel. The door is fitted to the room it belongs in — set, levelled, and anchored as the job’s scope specifies — with the wall and frame facts taken from the door manufacturer’s own requirements for that specific door.

Modular vault panel relocation & assembly support. Modular vaults travel as panels and are rebuilt on site. We relocate panel systems and support their reassembly, panel by panel, in the order the manufacturer specifies.

Antique & vintage vault door relocation. Older doors carry no spec sheet — they carry a maker’s plate and a century of weight. We move antique and vintage doors at their true weights, surveyed and planned piece by piece (see below).

Every job starts from the same intake: the door’s make and model or its dimensions and weight, the rating on its label or spec sheet if it has one, the room and wall type at both ends, the route between them, and the floor at placement.

## The weight reality

A vault door is the heaviest single object most buildings ever receive. Across the verified models in our vault door models dataset (#/datasets/vault-doors) — manufacturer-stated figures only, each with its evidence — door weights run from 1,225 to 1,610 lbs: a Liberty Beast residential door at 1,245 lbs, Fort Knox 82-series doors at 1,310 to 1,610 lbs, Overly’s federal Class 5 doors at about 1,225 to 1,269 lbs. Antique doors routinely run far heavier, and a door’s true weight — never a guess — is what the plan is built on.

Where a door’s weight falls in the 1,500 to 3,500 lb band, the job is planned under SIR — Structural Integrity Relocation — and the KIM-GS Protocol: the route is surveyed, the load path is protected, and the floor at placement is checked with a deflection analysis to L/360 before the door is committed to it. A floor that fails the check is a planning problem solved before move day, not a surprise on it. Doors above the band are scoped from their own facts — heavier rigging, engineered load paths — and doors below it are handled with the same careful method, at their true weight.

## The standards, in plain terms

Vault doors are bought against standards, and the standards are widely misquoted. Our vault security standards registry (#/datasets/vault-security) carries the figures from the standards’ own text; the short version is this.

UL 608 covers burglary-resistant vault doors and modular panels. It has exactly four classes — M, 1, 2, and 3 — rated by net working time against one identical attack basis (common mechanical tools, electric tools, cutting torches, or any combination): Class M resists 15 minutes, Class 1 resists 30, Class 2 resists 60, and Class 3 resists 120. Time is the only difference between the classes. And section 1.3 of the standard is plain: UL 608 does not cover attacks with the burning bar (thermal lance) or explosives — no UL 608 class is rated against explosives or a thermal lance, whatever a chart on the internet says. A class is legitimate only on a UL Certified door bearing the UL Mark; “built to UL 608” without the Mark is a manufacturer’s self-declaration, not a listing.

GSA Class 5 under AA-D-600D is the federal vault door specification, in three classes. Class 5-V (vault) resists 20 man-hours of surreptitious entry, 30 man-minutes of covert entry, and 10 man-minutes of forced entry — the hours/minutes distinction is the most common misquote in this field — and carries no ballistic requirement. Class 5-A (armory) drops the surreptitious requirement, keeping 30 man-minutes covert and 10 forced. Class 5-B is the ballistic class: the same entry figures as 5-V, plus ballistic resistance tested to SD-STD-01.01 Rev. G level 2 — and the specification names no test round, so any source that names one for Class 5-B is going beyond the spec.

The lock is a separate layer, with separate figures. Class 5-V and 5-B doors carry a lock meeting the federal lock specification FF-L-2740 (Style H hand-change or Style K key-change); Class 5-A’s lock is a UL 768 Group 1 lock. UL 768 lock groups: Group 1 resists expert manipulation for 20 working hours; Group 1R adds 20 hours of radiological resistance; Group 2M resists 2 hours; and Group 2 carries no hour figure in the standard at all — it requires a moderate degree of resistance, and any hour number attached to Group 2 is invented. FF-L-2740B, the federal electromechanical lock spec, requires 20 man-hours each against manipulation, radiological analysis, and emanations analysis, and 30 man-minutes against covert entry — and its locks are sold only to the Federal Government and authorized contractors, never as retail products. Time locks sit under UL 887, not UL 768.

## Installation

Installation begins before the door arrives: the route is surveyed, the structure at placement is checked, and the door’s own manufacturer requirements for wall, frame, and opening govern the door-specific facts — we do not substitute generic engineering claims for the manufacturer’s specification for your door. On the day: the door is brought in along the protected route, set into its opening, levelled, and anchored as scoped. Vault and safe contents are emptied by the customer before any move or installation — always. And one boundary, stated plainly: we provide no locksmith or combination services. Combination changes, lock opening, and lock replacement are locksmith and manufacturer work; our work is the door’s movement, placement, and installation.

## Antique & vintage doors

An antique vault door is identified by its maker’s plate, not a model number. We record the maker, the door’s measured dimensions, and its true weight — vintage doors routinely exceed modern residential doors by a wide margin — and plan the move with the same care we give antiques and museum pieces: condition noted before the move, protection matched to the finish, and a route planned for a piece that cannot be replaced. Where an old door is being fitted into a room, the installation scope is planned from the door’s own facts and the room’s structure, surveyed in advance.

## Who this is for

Banks and credit unions fitting out or retiring a vault; jewelers and pharmacies building secure rooms; armories and ranges; collectors and safe-room homeowners buying a residential door that weighs as much as a car; estates settling a property with a door in it. If the object is a vault door or a high-security enclosure — new, reconditioned, or a hundred years old — this is the service that moves and installs it.

## What to tell us for a quote

The make and model, or the door’s dimensions and weight; the rating from the door’s label or spec sheet, if it has one; the room and wall type where it sits and where it is going; the route at both ends (stairs, turns, doorways); the floor at placement; and the lock’s condition as you know it. With those facts we review the full scope — distance, manpower, equipment — and price the job at one flat rate in writing. Get a flat rate quote (#/quote).

## Questions, answered

What do the UL 608 vault door classes mean?

UL 608 has four classes — M, 1, 2, and 3 — rated by net working time against the same attack basis of common mechanical tools, electric tools, and cutting torches: Class M resists 15 minutes, Class 1 resists 30 minutes, Class 2 resists 60 minutes, and Class 3 resists 120 minutes. Time is the only difference between classes, and a class counts only on a UL Certified door bearing the UL Mark.

Is a GSA Class 5-V vault door bulletproof?

No. Under AA-D-600D, Class 5-V resists 20 man-hours of surreptitious entry, 30 man-minutes of covert entry, and 10 man-minutes of forced entry, with no ballistic requirement. Ballistic resistance belongs to Class 5-B, tested to SD-STD-01.01 Rev. G level 2 — and the specification names no test round.

How much does a vault door weigh?

It depends on the door. Across the verified manufacturer-stated models in our vault door models dataset, weights run from 1,225 to 1,610 lbs — residential doors around 1,245 to 1,610 lbs and federal Class 5 doors at about 1,225 to 1,269 lbs. Antique doors often weigh much more. Your door’s stated or measured weight is what its move is planned from.

Do you install vault doors of any size?

Yes. Installation is offered at any size — a residential safe-room door, a GSA Class 5 door, or a modular vault assembled panel by panel — with the door-specific wall and frame facts taken from the manufacturer’s requirements for that door.

Does my floor need a check before a vault door is installed?

For a door in the 1,500 to 3,500 lb band, yes: the placement floor is checked with a deflection analysis to L/360 under SIR before the door is committed to it. Lighter and heavier doors are assessed from their own weight and the floor’s construction, surveyed in advance.

Do I need to empty the vault before the door is moved or installed?

Yes — vault and safe contents are emptied by the customer before any move or installation, always. We move and install the door and the enclosure, never their contents.

Can you change my vault door’s combination or replace its lock?

No. We provide no locksmith or combination services — combination changes, lock opening, and lock replacement are locksmith and manufacturer work. Our work is the door’s delivery, relocation, and installation.

What does vault door moving or installation cost?

Every job is reviewed in full — the door, its weight and class, the route at both ends, the floor, manpower, and equipment — and priced at one flat rate in writing before the job. There is no per-hour meter running on a vault door.

Can an antique vault door be relocated?

Yes. Antique and vintage doors are identified from the maker’s plate, weighed honestly — they routinely exceed modern doors — and moved with antique-grade care: condition noted first, finishes protected, and the route planned for a piece that cannot be replaced.

Which areas do you serve for vault door work?

Both branches dispatch vault door work: The Flat Rate Movers in Winchester, VA for the Shenandoah Valley side, and Flat Rate Movers Martinsburg WV for Berkeley County and the Eastern Panhandle, along the I-81, I-66, and I-70 corridors. One number reaches both: +1-540-422-2153.

### Hoarding Cleanup & Cleanout

Hoarding cleanup and whole-property cleanout quoted at one flat rate in writing after an in-person assessment — the crew sorts with the client or family (keep, donate, discard), handles heavy contents as heavy work, performs credentialed scope through the credentialed contractors the company engages, offers emergency response, and works discreetly, dispatched from Winchester, VA and Martinsburg, WV.

Primary page: https://theflatratemovers.com/hoarding-cleanup/

🧹 HOARDING CLEANUP & CLEANOUT — SHENANDOAH VALLEY · EASTERN PANHANDLE

# Hoarding Cleanup & Cleanout
A hoarding cleanout is heavy, emotional, and usually on a deadline — a parent’s house to settle, a code notice with a date on it, a sale that cannot close. We do the whole job: surveyed in advance, sorted with the family, heavy contents handled as heavy work, and quoted at one flat rate in writing before anything is touched. Emergency response is offered, and the work is done discreetly.

Get My Flat Rate Quote (#/quote)

## What we do

Whole-property hoarding cleanouts. Basements, garages, and whole houses cleared room by room — the contents sorted with the client or the family into keep, donate, and discard, then hauled out to donation, recycling, and lawful disposal. Nothing leaves that the family has not decided on.

Heavy contents, handled as heavy work. Hoarded homes hold the heaviest household contents there are — furniture, appliances, safes, stoves, packed shelving. They are moved with the same structural care this company applies to its heavy work: paths and floors protected, weight handled as weight, never dragged. A safe in the house is emptied first, always, and moved the way we move safes.

Credentialed scope, under the same engagement. Where a property involves biohazard conditions or other regulated scope, that scope is performed by the credentialed contractors we engage for it — under the same written flat rate and the same job, not a second company you have to find.

Emergency response. When the deadline is a fire-marshal or code-enforcement date, or a family emergency, cleanouts are dispatched on the fastest available schedule.

Discretion, as a working practice. No signage about the job, no discussion of the property with neighbors or anyone outside it, and a crew that understands whose home this is. Many of our clients are families in a hard week; the work is handled that way.

## The situations we are called for

After a death in the family. The most common call. A parent’s home has to be emptied and settled or sold, the condition was discovered late, and the family is grieving, often from out of town. We work to the family’s decisions — documents, photographs, and valuables are set aside before a room is cleared — and the property is left emptied and swept, ready for probate, listing, or handover.

A code-enforcement or fire-marshal deadline. A notice arrives with a correction deadline and fines, liens, or condemnation behind it. Martinsburg enforces the 2015 International Property Maintenance Code, whose process is a confirmed violation, a correction order, and a deadline; Alexandria, Virginia’s published hoarding-response procedure runs the same way — document the conditions, involve code, fire, and adult protective services, and give written notice with deadlines. A cleanout scoped in writing, with the rooms documented before and after, is the answer that satisfies an inspector.

Before selling. Sellers and heirs choose between selling as-is — cash buyers price the cleanout into a lower offer and can close in weeks — and cleaning out first, then listing, which takes longer and typically brings a stronger price. Market reporting on hoarded-house sales is consistent that the longest part of a cleanout is usually the family’s keep-and-discard decisions, not the hauling. We do the hauling and the heavy work; the decisions stay yours, at your pace or your deadline’s.

Landlords and property managers. A hoarded unit is a fire, pest, and inspection risk, and lease and fair-housing constraints apply to how it is handled. We restore the unit to an emptied, swept condition the owner can act on, with the tenant’s property decisions documented as the lease requires.

Helping a parent or family member. When the person still lives in the home, the cleanout runs at their pace and with their decisions in front — safety first (a working kitchen, clear exits, a safe path to the bathroom), dignity throughout.

## How a cleanout runs

1. Assessment and a written flat rate. The property is walked and the full scope — rooms, density, heavy items, hazardous conditions, disposal routes — is reviewed in full, then quoted at one flat rate in writing before any work begins. No hourly billing, and no by-the-truckload surprises.

2. The sort is the client’s. Keep, donate, discard — the family decides. The crew works to the agreed sort, setting aside documents, photographs, valuables, and anything flagged before a room is cleared.

3. Heavy items handled as heavy work. Furniture, appliances, safes, and stoves move under the company’s heavy-work method, with floors and paths protected. Contents are emptied from safes before they move, as on every safe job.

4. Credentialed scope through engaged contractors. Biohazard conditions and other regulated scope are performed by the credentialed contractors the company engages, inside the same engagement.

5. Haul-out and lawful disposal. Cleared contents leave by the agreed routes — donation for usable goods, recycling for recyclable material, lawful disposal for the remainder.

6. Handover: emptied and swept. Rooms are left emptied and broom-swept, retained shelving and fixtures in place — the condition a family, a listing agent, or a code inspector can act on.

## A real cleanout — Chantilly, Virginia

This is our own work, photographed on the job: a basement and garage cleanout in Chantilly, Virginia. The rooms held hoarding-density contents — hundreds of prescription bottles, paints, solvents and household chemicals, furniture, a washing machine, and a large wood stove. Everything was sorted and hauled to a roll-off container, and the rooms were left emptied and swept, shelving retained in place. No client name or address is published — the job is documented as work evidence, the way our clients’ privacy is always handled.

## What it costs — stated honestly

Every cleanout is surveyed and quoted at one flat rate in writing before work begins — priced from the actual scope: rooms, density, heavy items, hazardous conditions, and disposal routes. We publish no per-square-foot range and no day rate, because a number invented before anyone has walked the property is not a price, it is a guess with a dollar sign.

For market context, the published figures a search will show you are vendor figures, not standards: one dumpster-rental vendor’s guides cite $0.75 to $2.50 per square foot of affected living space, and $1,000 to $2,000 per day; a national junk-removal brand prices by the fraction of a truck your load fills. Treat all of them as other companies’ marketing numbers. Ours is the written flat rate for your property, agreed before the job — and if you would rather be billed by the hour, hourly pricing is available when a client asks for it.

## The research behind the work

How common this is. The International OCD Foundation puts hoarding disorder at an estimated 2% to 6% of the population, roughly three times more common in older adults, with about 75% of people who hoard also living with a co-occurring mental-health condition, most commonly depression. A 2019 meta-analysis pooling 11 studies and 53,378 participants found a pooled prevalence of 2.5%. This is not a rare condition, and a family dealing with it is not alone in it.

Why fire services treat it as an emergency. NFPA’s guidance to the fire service is plain: fire departments are experiencing serious fires, injuries, and deaths as the result of compulsive hoarding behavior; blocked exits prevent escape; and obstructed exits, falling objects, and excessive fire loading that can lead to collapse put responding firefighters at risk. That is why a code or fire-marshal notice is a deadline we work to, not a suggestion.

Why the written scope matters. There is no industry-wide standard for hoarding cleanups — the restoration trade press has said so outright. In a field with no standard, the written scope agreed before work begins is the buyer’s protection: what is sorted, what is hauled, what is disposed of and where, and the one flat rate it is done for. Ours is in writing, every time.

Insurance. Homeowners insurance usually does not cover hoarding cleanup — the condition is treated as arising from negligence or maintenance, and some policies exclude it. Ask your own carrier about your policy; do not count on coverage when you plan.

The full research layer — every claim with its source and its standing — is published as the hoarding cleanup dataset (#/datasets/hoarding-cleanup).

## Questions, answered

How much does a hoarding cleanout cost?

It is priced per property, not per formula. We walk the property, review the full scope — rooms, density, heavy items, hazardous conditions, disposal — and quote one flat rate in writing before work begins. Published per-square-foot and per-day figures online are other vendors’ marketing numbers; we do not publish a range we have not surveyed.

How long does a cleanout take?

Most of the time in a cleanout is the sort — the family’s keep, donate, and discard decisions — not the hauling. A scoped job is scheduled against your deadline, and emergency-response calls are dispatched on the fastest available schedule.

Do family members have to be there, and who decides what is thrown away?

The decisions are the client’s or the family’s, always — in person, or by an agreed plan for families working from out of town. Documents, photographs, and valuables are set aside before any room is cleared, and nothing is discarded outside the agreed sort.

What if the property has biohazard conditions?

That scope is performed by the credentialed contractors we engage for it, under the same engagement and the same written flat rate. Tell us what you know about the property’s condition when you call, and it is planned into the scope from the start.

Can you respond to a code-enforcement or fire-marshal deadline?

Yes — emergency response is offered, and a dated notice is the first thing to tell us about. The cleanout is scoped in writing and the rooms documented, which is what an inspector’s re-inspection needs to see.

Will the neighbors know what is happening?

The work is discreet by practice: no signage about the job, no discussion of the property with anyone outside it. What a passerby sees is a crew clearing a house — the circumstances stay private.

Does homeowners insurance pay for hoarding cleanup?

Usually not — insurers generally treat hoarding as a maintenance condition rather than a covered loss, and some policies exclude it. Check your own policy with your carrier; plan on the written flat rate, not on coverage.

What happens to the things that are removed?

Usable goods go to donation, recyclable material to recycling, and the remainder to lawful disposal, by the routes agreed in the written scope. In the Chantilly cleanout the haul filled a roll-off container.

There is a safe / appliances / heavy furniture in the house. Can you take those too?

Yes — heavy contents are part of the service and are handled as heavy work. A safe is emptied first, always, and moved with the same method we move safes with professionally.

How do I start?

Call +1-540-422-2153 or get a flat rate quote (#/quote). Tell us the property’s location, the rooms involved, any deadline you are under, and anything heavy or hazardous you know about. We schedule the assessment, and the written flat rate follows from the walk-through.

### Is it really one flat rate?
Yes. Your move is quoted as one flat price, agreed in writing before move day — we do not bill by the hour. Our guarantee: Guaranteed Flat Rate or Your Move is Free!

### What weights need SIR?
Assets of 1,500 to 3,500 lbs — safes, medical devices, cryogenic equipment, pianos and antiques — are planned under SIR and the KIM-GS Protocol, with a floor-deflection check to L/360 before anything lifts.

### What is ISPM 15?
The International Standards for Phytosanitary Measures No. 15 — the global rule for wood packaging in export. Our export crates are built from compliant, treated, marked wood so shipments clear customs.

## In depth — FAQ — Questions, Answered
Frequently asked questions about flat-rate moving, SIR heavy-asset moves, ISPM 15 export packing, service areas, hours and the Short/Detailed quote toggle.

### The answers, in full
Is it really one flat rate?

Yes. Every job is reviewed in full — scope, distance, manpower, equipment — and priced at one flat rate in writing before move day. hourly pricing is available when a client asks for it and no meter running on the day. Guaranteed Flat Rate or Your Move is Free!

What weights need SIR?

High-mass assets of 1,500 to 3,500 lbs move under SIR — Structural Integrity Relocation — and the KIM-GS Protocol: the route and clearances are surveyed, the floor at placement is checked to an L/360 deflection standard, and the load is spread and protected. Safes under 1,500 lbs are handled the same careful way.

What is ISPM 15?

ISPM 15 is the international standard for wood packaging in export shipments — heat treatment to 56 °C for 30 minutes at the core, with the IPPC mark. Export packing and custom crating here are built to that standard so shipments clear customs without the packaging becoming the problem.

Where do you serve?

From two branches: Winchester, VA (32 published areas across the Shenandoah Valley, Frederick and Loudoun counties and the I-81 / I-66 corridors) and Martinsburg, WV (35 published areas across the Eastern Panhandle and into Maryland) — 53 published areas in all, 14 of them shared. Long-distance and heavy-asset work runs far beyond the home footprint.

How are you rated on Google?

Per branch, and never blended: Winchester 5.0 from 2 reviews; Martinsburg 4.7 from 6 reviews. Much of the work is high-value and privacy-sensitive, and those clients do not review publicly — the count is small because the work is private, not because the work is rare.

- **The Flat Rate Movers — FF&E Logistics Process Chain Dataset** — The process chain for an FF&E logistics project. Step 0, scope alignment: the buyer or project team supplies the project address, vendor and purchase-order references when available, FF&E schedule, room matrix, floor plans, installation drawings, storage interval, access rules, and the boundary between logistics support and licensed or technical work; the full scope is reviewed and quoted at one flat rate. Step 1, purchase-order receiving: staggered vendor shipments are received as one project stream rather than unrelated freight. Step 2, dock inventory and condition: freight is counted and inventoried as it crosses the dock, tied to project and purchase-order references where supplied, and labeled and inventory-tagged to its room or phase destination, with visible damage, shortages, overages, and discrepancies recorded as receiving exceptions while the delivery record is fresh. Step 3, warehousing: received product is held in leased space — furniture-padded or shrink-wrapped as the item requires, with corner and edge protectors on finished surfaces — under the company's published storage basis — 30-day minimum, customer access, pricing per job, monthly, or by volume — until the building sequence calls for it. Step 4, sequence and pull: product is pulled by model room, floor, room number, department, classroom, office, or phase, not by the order in which vendor trucks arrived. Step 5, site delivery: the sequence moves to the site around dock and elevator reservations, active trades, protected routes, and occupied areas. Step 6, installation support: crews unpack, assemble, place, and level FF&E within the logistics scope — working with furniture pads under pieces in motion and corner protectors on finished edges — and set in place items that do not require licensed-trade connection or manufacturer commissioning. Step 7, packaging and debris removal: packaging generated by the delivered FF&E is removed within the project scope. Step 8, punch and opening readiness: completed areas, outstanding items, and exceptions are walked and documented so the project team can see what is finished and what remains open. Domain reference (Bailey's Workplace FF&E guide, labeled as such): mature programs often coordinate delivery through a tentative window several weeks out, a firmer confirmation seven to ten days out, and a final confirmation 72 hours ahead; the company's project gates are set in the written scope with the GC or project team, not promised as universal lead times. Download: https://theflatratemovers.com/datasets-ffe-logistics.json · Landing: https://theflatratemovers.com/datasets/ffe-logistics/
- **The Flat Rate Movers — Final-Mile Delivery Process Chain Dataset** — The process chain for a final-mile delivery. Company chain (published): freight arrives by container, truck or warehouse staging; it is unloaded and inventoried as it crosses the dock; staged on the warehouse floor, deconsolidated or cross-docked where a shipment needs to split or change vehicles, and reworked where needed; then delivered in on the final mile — brought in on a planned route, set in its final position, packaging removed, and condition verified with the recipient before the crew leaves. Domain reference (the general final-mile chain, labeled as such): linehaul or container arrival at a regional facility; sort and route planning; appointment scheduling with the recipient; a pre-delivery access check (doorways, stairs, elevators); two-person inside delivery for big-and-bulky freight; placement, inspection and proof of delivery. The domain sequence describes how final-mile delivery is generally worked; the company's published chain above is the company's own. - **The Flat Rate Movers — Freight Rework Process Chain Dataset** — The published process chain for a freight rework, step by step. Step 1, intake: the call records what happened, where the truck is, what the freight is, and photos from the driver when available; the job is scoped and quoted at one flat rate before work begins, with emergency and after-hours work quoted at the emergency premium. Step 2, site decision: the work happens where the job requires — the company's leased space, the receiver's dock, or a yard. Step 3, stabilize and open: the trailer is opened under control, because a shifted load can fall at the doors, and the freight is stabilized before anyone works inside the box. Step 4, document before touching: photographs of the load as found, counts against the bill of lading, damage noted — the record that protects the carrier's and shipper's claim position. Step 5, unload: freight is removed in sequence; damaged cases are pulled and set aside, never buried back into the load. Step 6, sort and segregate: freight is sorted by SKU, purchase order or destination as the receiver requires, and good freight is separated from overage, shortage and damage freight. Step 7, rebuild: freight is restacked to the receiver's Ti/Hi pattern and stack height, repalletized onto sound pallets, failed packaging replaced where needed, and the load re-wrapped and secured; materials are used at the step that needs them — pallets, stretch wrap, corner protection, dunnage and air bags, strapping — purchased per project. Step 8, weight correction: for axle work, freight is repositioned along the box and redistributed between axles, verified against the scale ticket where a scale is part of the job. Step 9, reload and secure: freight is reloaded in delivery sequence and secured so the aggregate working load limit of the tiedowns reaches at least one-half the cargo weight and tiedown counts meet the federal cargo securement standard recorded in the compliance node. Step 10, document and hand back: after-photos, final counts, bill-of-lading notation of the work performed, and receiver or carrier sign-off, so the driver rolls with paperwork that matches the freight. The planned-work chains run through the same floor discipline: a cross-dock moves freight receiving dock to shipping dock, sorted and consolidated, typically inside 24 hours; a transload unloads the inbound mode — container or railcar — repalletizes or sorts floor-loaded freight, stages it briefly where the job requires, and builds the outbound truck load. Download: https://theflatratemovers.com/datasets-freight-rework.json · Landing: https://theflatratemovers.com/datasets/freight-rework/

Furniture: sofas, sectionals, recliners, dressers, wardrobes, dining sets, bed frames, and entertainment centers — carried out whole where the path allows, taken apart when a piece must come apart to leave safely. Mattresses and box springs: bagged or wrapped for the carry out, and routed to facilities that accept them. Appliances: washers, dryers, ranges, dishwashers, refrigerators, freezers, and water heaters — disconnected from their hookups as part of the pickup where the connection is a standard household connection; appliances that contain refrigerant are routed so the refrigerant is recovered by certified technicians before processing, under the federal rule recorded in the compliance node. Electronics and e-waste: televisions, computers, and small electronics, routed to electronics recycling. Exercise equipment: treadmills, ellipticals, weight benches, and racks — taken apart for the carry when needed. Hot tubs and spas: the tub is drained and disconnected from power and water before the appointment; the crew cuts and hauls the shell in sections. Yard debris: brush, branches, fencing, and playsets. Renovation and construction debris: drywall, lumber, plywood, flooring, carpet, cabinets, countertops, and fixtures — dense material such as concrete, brick, and soil is planned by weight, because weight, not space, governs how much a truck can carry in one load. Whole-property material: bagged household junk and accumulated contents from garages, basements, attics, estates, evictions, and office cleanouts. Access is recorded at the survey — stairs, long carries, elevators, and tight doorways are part of the scope the flat rate is written against, never a surprise added on the day. Download: https://theflatratemovers.com/datasets-junk-removal.json · Landing: https://theflatratemovers.com/datasets/junk-removal/
- **Local Graph Registry Dataset — Scope** — What this registry is and the rules it runs on. The graph’s center (Google) resolves both branches correctly; the graph’s edges (aggregators, directories, stale scrapes) corrupt them — and the edges are the layer answer engines and secondary directories actually read. This dataset is the permanent corrections worklist for that layer: branch truth generated from the estate; every public record as a field-level row with a status from a controlled vocabulary; propagation parents so a downstream row is never demanded fixed before its upstream; corrected-live earned only on direct-fetch proof; verification aging flagged, never silently trusted; collisions catalogued DO-NOT-TOUCH; and the owner’s action list generated from the rows it blocks so it cannot drift. - **Move Sizes & Access Operations** — Move sizes and access operations for local and regional moves: the size bands, dwelling types, and access conditions that shape a local quote. Size bands, as demand shapes rather than company products: studio and one-bedroom homes, small jobs and partial loads, two-to-three-bedroom homes, four-plus-bedroom homes, and small offices. Dwelling and premises types: apartments, condos, townhomes, houses, estates, offices, and shops. Access conditions are quote inputs, never capability claims: stairs, elevator type and reservation, doorway and hallway width, parking and loading zones, long carry distance, building hours, and HOA rules. Staging runs through the driveway, yard, garage, or loading zone. Market reference data, labeled as such and never company times or prices: market guides plan studio and one-bedroom moves at roughly 3 to 5 hours with 2 movers, two-to-three-bedroom homes at 5 to 8 hours with 2 to 3 movers, and four-plus-bedroom homes at 8 to 12 hours with 3 to 4 movers; walk-up stairs, tight turns, elevator reservation windows, parking permits, and building move windows are the access factors that move a quote. The company publishes homes and businesses, with homeowners, renters, families, and seniors named on the branch pages, and no size-specific crew, equipment, minimum, or access capability is claimed anywhere in this dataset — the survey governs each job. - **Distance Bands & Shipment Sizes** — Distance bands and shipment sizes for long-distance moving — the reference taxonomy every long-distance quote is built from. Distance bands: local (same area, same day — the local and regional category, not this service); regional (beyond local, inside the corridor network — cross-referenced to the local and regional and corridor pages); interstate (across a state line, where federal household-goods rules under 49 CFR Part 375 apply — the company's pages publish interstate scope from both branches, and the destination lanes in the route network dataset run on it); cross-country (coast-to-coast or multi-day linehaul, typically 1,500+ miles — defended at positions 4.0 to 7.1 in the company's Search Console record); and destination-lane (a named origin-to-destination lane, such as Virginia to Florida). Shipment size bands, as typical weights from published mover guides, labeled domain reference and never company figures: studio and one-bedroom homes at 2,000 to 3,500 lbs, where consolidation economics dominate; two-bedroom homes at 4,000 to 6,000 lbs, the most common long-distance band; three-bedroom homes at 6,000 to 9,000 lbs, where accessorials — stairs, long carry, shuttle — start to dominate the variance; four-plus-bedroom homes at 9,000 lbs and up, often 11,000 to 15,000 lbs, where weight accuracy and delivery-window planning dominate. A single heavy piece is not a household shipment band at all: pieces of 1,500 to 3,500 lbs move under the published SIR band, cross-referenced to the SIR heavy-asset and gun-safe categories. Weight times distance is the linehaul basis, and every band feeds the cost drivers in the commercial terms dataset; the survey governs each move. - **Lab Move Sequence & Custody Operations** — The sequence and custody model for a medical or laboratory move — the order of operations and the documentation at each hand-off. Planning phase: unit inventory with weights and dimensions; route survey at origin and destination (door, corridor, elevator and stair measurements); floor check against L/360 on the load path; crate plan for fragile components. Coordination phase: the move calendar is set against the vendor's de-installation window and the facility's access, hours and infection-control routing rules; the facility EHS decontamination sign-off is received where required — a document the facility issues about its own equipment, recorded in the move file, never issued by the mover. Execution phase: vendor technicians perform the technical de-installation; the crew supports with positioning and rigging; each unit's condition is documented as it is released, packed or crated, and sealed; seals and condition records travel with the load; at destination each unit is unsealed, condition-checked against the origin record, placed and leveled. Close-out phase: placement is verified with the facility's team and the vendor's recommissioning schedule takes over. Custody principle: at every point, one named party holds each unit — facility, vendor, or mover — and the hand-offs are the documented moments. What this dataset does not describe: any technical procedure on the equipment itself (disconnection, draining, preparation, reconnection, calibration), which belongs to the vendor and is recorded here only as a scheduling gate. Download: https://theflatratemovers.com/datasets-medical-lab-relocation.json · Landing: https://theflatratemovers.com/datasets/medical-lab-relocation/

- **Storage Interval & Access Operations** — Storage interval and access operations — the reference bands every move-with-storage plan is built from. - **The Flat Rate Movers — Corridor Dispatch Process Chain Dataset** — The process chain for a corridor move. Company chain (published): the job is surveyed and quoted at one flat rate in writing before move day; dispatch is planned by route, access and load — which corridor carries the move (I-81 north–south, I-66 east toward Northern Virginia and DC, or I-70 toward Maryland), which junction it turns at, and which of the two corridor branches dispatches it; the crew starts on the corridor, so the run carries less deadhead time; freight moves run through the company's own warehouse and transload floor where a shipment needs staging, deconsolidation or a change of vehicle; the move is delivered in, placed, and verified at the destination end — and where either end holds a heavy asset of 1,500 to 3,500 lbs, the SIR survey and L/360 floor check join the chain before the run is scheduled. Domain reference (how corridor-based dispatch generally works, labeled as such): a carrier positioned on a freight corridor assigns each job to the branch nearest the freight, selects the route by destination corridor rather than by map distance alone, sequences pickups and deliveries along the corridor to cut empty miles, and uses warehouse staging at corridor junctions to join port, linehaul and final-mile legs. The domain sequence describes the general model; the company's published chain above is the company's own.
